0.title: 2 Chronicles: If My People
0.overview:
The second half of the Chronicler's great history opens at the zenith of Israel's glory and closes on the edge of a darkness that swallowed a nation. Solomon sits on David's throne, the ark is carried to the new-built temple, fire falls from heaven on the first sacrifices, and the glory-cloud fills the house so the priests cannot stand to minister. By the last chapter, that same temple lies in ashes, the covenant people are marched to Babylon, and the land keeps its sabbaths at last — the only way it could get them, through the silence of exile.

Yet 2 Chronicles is not a tragedy. It is a theology of history, written for a people who have come home from exile and are asking the hardest question history can pose: Why did it all collapse, and is there still hope? The Chronicler answers with a governing text placed at dead center — 7:14, God's response to Solomon's great prayer of dedication: If my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land. Every king who follows is measured against that four-fold call: humble yourself, pray, seek my face, turn. The kings who do these things — Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joash, Hezekiah, Josiah — see God's hand move on their behalf. The kings who despise them — Rehoboam, Ahaz, Manasseh in his long wickedness, Jehoiakim, Zedekiah — drag the nation toward the abyss.

The Chronicler is not writing neutral history. He is a preacher with a congregation of returned exiles who need to understand not merely what happened but why, and more urgently, whether the covenant is still alive. His answer is that it is — because the God who sent the nation into exile is the same God who moved the heart of Cyrus to let his people go up. The last word of 2 Chronicles — and of the entire Hebrew Bible in the Jewish canonical order — is ya'al: let him go up. The exile is not the final word. Ascent is.

Key theological motifs: (1) The temple as the meeting-place of heaven and earth, pointing forward to Christ as the true temple (John 2:19–21). (2) Solomon's prayer of dedication as a sustained theology of access to God, pointing forward to Christ's high-priestly prayer in John 17. (3) The ma'al principle — breach of faith explains every disaster; the Hebrew word for unfaithful treachery appears throughout as the Chronicler's diagnostic for national ruin. (4) "The eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him" (16:9) — the book's most arresting statement of divine providence. (5) The reform-king pattern, each faithful king prefiguring the ultimate Reformer who will cleanse the true temple and inaugurate the final Passover.

Dale Ralph Davis observes that Chronicles is above all a book about worship — not worship as a warm feeling but worship as the organizing principle of a nation's life. When the temple is right, the nation is right. When the temple is neglected, everything else falls. The Chronicler's central conviction is that Israel's deepest problem was never political or military — it was liturgical. They forgot how to come to God. And that, the returning exiles needed to hear, is still the only issue that matters.

1.title: Ask What I Shall Give You
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Solomon the son of David established himself in his kingdom, and the LORD his God was with him and made him exceedingly great.<sup>2</sup>Solomon spoke to all Israel, to the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, to the judges, and to all the leaders in all Israel, the heads of fathers' houses.<sup>3</sup>And Solomon, and all the assembly with him, went to the high place that was at Gibeon, for the tent of meeting of God, which Moses the servant of the LORD had made in the wilderness, was there.<sup>4</sup>(But David had brought up the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim to the place that David had prepared for it, for he had pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem.)<sup>5</sup>Moreover, the bronze altar that Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, had made, was there before the tabernacle of the LORD. And Solomon and the assembly sought it out.<sup>6</sup>And Solomon went up there to the bronze altar before the LORD, which was at the tent of meeting, and offered a thousand burnt offerings on it.<sup>7</sup>In that night God appeared to Solomon, and said to him, "Ask what I shall give you."<sup>8</sup>And Solomon said to God, "You have shown great and steadfast love to David my father, and have made me king in his place.<sup>9</sup>O LORD God, let your word to David my father be now fulfilled, for you have made me king over a people as numerous as the dust of the earth.<sup>10</sup>Give me now wisdom and knowledge to go out and come in before this people, for who can govern this people of yours, which is so great?"<sup>11</sup>God answered Solomon, "Because this was in your heart, and you have not asked for possessions, wealth, honor, or the life of those who hate you, and have not even asked for long life, but have asked for wisdom and knowledge for yourself that you may govern my people over whom I have made you king,<sup>12</sup>wisdom and knowledge are granted to you. I will also give you riches, possessions, and honor, such as none of the kings had who were before you, and none after you shall have the like."<sup>13</sup>So Solomon came from the high place at Gibeon, from before the tent of meeting, to Jerusalem. And he reigned over Israel.<sup>14</sup>Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.<sup>15</sup>And the king made silver and gold as common in Jerusalem as stone, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah.<sup>16</sup>And Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt and Kue, and the king's traders would buy them from Kue for a price.<sup>17</sup>They imported a chariot from Egypt for 600 shekels of silver, and a horse for 150. Likewise through them these were exported to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Syria.
1.overview:
Solomon secures the throne, and God is named as the reason he is great (v. 1). He takes the whole nation to Gibeon, where the tabernacle Moses made and Bezalel's bronze altar are standing, and offers a thousand burnt offerings (vv. 2-6) — the ark meanwhile being in a separate tent in Jerusalem (v. 4). That night God says Ask what I shall give you, and Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge to lead a people he calls God's rather than his own; God grants it and adds the riches he did not ask for (vv. 7-13). The chapter closes with 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, imported from Egypt (vv. 14-17).

Kings tells how Solomon established himself — four men dead and one priest exiled. Chronicles prints none of it, in the same way it printed the setting of David's worst night and left the night out.
1.theology:
Solomon prays the way his father prayed. David, given the covenant, asked God to do as you have spoken; Solomon, given a blank cheque, says let your word to David my father be now fulfilled. Neither invents a request. Both take what God has already said and hand it back as a petition, which is what praying becomes once a person has listened.

And the chapter closes on an unresolved tension the Chronicler will not resolve for us. The horses and the silver are verse 12 coming true. The horses are also the thing Deuteronomy 17 forbade the king to accumulate, from the country it named. Both statements are in the text, neither is retracted, and the book that follows is largely the working out of what happens when a blessing is received on the wrong terms.
1.examples:
Ask what I shall give you is not a test with a right answer to be worked out. It came at night, without warning, and what came out of Solomon was simply what was in him — which is what God says when he answers: because this was in your heart.

He asked for the competence to lead this people of yours. Months into a reign he had already stopped calling the nation his own, and the request he made followed from that one word.

The altar he offered on had been made in a desert four hundred years earlier by a man God filled with his Spirit for the job. The richest king Israel ever had did not replace it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The King Goes to Gibeon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon the son of David established himself in his kingdom, and the LORD his God was with him and made him exceedingly great (v. 1) — and the first thing he does with the throne is summon the whole nation and take it to worship (v. 2). They go to Gibeon, for the tent of meeting of God, which Moses the servant of the LORD had made in the wilderness, was there (v. 3), while the ark stands in a tent David pitched in Jerusalem (v. 4). The altar in front of the tabernacle is named: the bronze one that Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, had made (v. 5). Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings on it (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's worship is still in two places, as it has been since the ark came up the hill. The new king goes first to the half that has the altar, and the whole book from here is about the day the two halves come under one roof.
verseByVerse.examples: The altar he sacrifices on was made in the wilderness by a craftsman God filled with his Spirit, and it is roughly four hundred years old. Nobody replaced it with something grander when the money arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon the son of David established himself in his kingdom, and the LORD his God was with him and made him exceedingly great. Solomon spoke to all Israel, to the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, to the judges, and to all the leaders in all Israel, the heads of fathers' houses. And Solomon, and all the assembly with him, went to the high place that was at Gibeon, for the tent of meeting of God, which Moses the servant of the LORD had made in the wilderness, was there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon the son of David established himself in his kingdom.

The verb means to make oneself strong, and the book of Kings spends a whole chapter telling how. Adonijah asked for the wrong woman and was executed. Joab ran to the tent of the LORD and took hold of the horns of the altar and was killed there anyway. Abiathar was sent home to his fields, and Shimei was penned inside Jerusalem for three years and then killed for crossing a valley to fetch a runaway slave.

None of that is here. This writer has done it before: he printed the sentence about the spring when kings go out to battle and left the roof and the letter and Uriah out of it. He is not writing a life of Solomon. He is writing how Israel came to have a temple, and the purge that secured the throne is not part of that story.

What he does print is the clause he printed over David's whole reign: and the LORD his God was with him and made him exceedingly great. The greatness is reported and the cause is named, and the cause is not the man.

Then the first act of the reign, and it is not a coronation feast or a building programme. He calls in every commander, judge and head of a family in the country and takes the whole assembly six miles north-west to a hill at Gibeon — for the tent of meeting of God, which Moses the servant of the LORD had made in the wilderness, was there.

That tent had been standing somewhere in Israel for four centuries. It had been at Sinai, in the wilderness, at Gilgal, at Shiloh, at Nob, and now on a height outside Jerusalem, and the young king's first official journey is to go and stand in front of it.

verseByVerse.quote: (But David had brought up the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim to the place that David had prepared for it, for he had pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem.) Moreover, the bronze altar that Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, had made, was there before the tabernacle of the LORD. And Solomon and the assembly sought it out. And Solomon went up there to the bronze altar before the LORD, which was at the tent of meeting, and offered a thousand burnt offerings on it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a parenthesis, and the Chronicler put it there because he knew the question it answers.

(But David had brought up the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim to the place that David had prepared for it, for he had pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem.)

Why is the king worshipping at a high place six miles from his capital when the ark of the covenant is in the city? Because Israel's worship has been split in two for a generation. The throne of God is in a tent on Zion with a choir round it and no altar; the tabernacle Moses made is at Gibeon with the bronze altar in front of it and an empty Most Holy Place. Neither site is whole. Both are obedient. Only this book tells us so, and everything from here to chapter 7 is about closing the gap.

Then the altar is identified, and the detail is this book's own. Moreover, the bronze altar that Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, had made, was there before the tabernacle of the LORD.

Bezalel is the craftsman God named to Moses at Sinai and filled with his Spirit to design the tabernacle — the first man in Scripture of whom that is said. The altar he beat out of bronze in a desert is still in service four hundred years later, and a king with more money than any of his predecessors comes and offers on it rather than commissioning a better one.

A thousand burnt offerings go up. Not peace offerings, which are shared and eaten — burnt offerings, which are consumed whole and leave the worshipper nothing. It is an absurd quantity, and it is the right way for a reign to open: the new king spends a day giving away what he will never get back.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — Ask What I Shall Give You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: That night God says Ask what I shall give you (v. 7). Solomon begins not with a request but with a debt — you have shown great and steadfast love to David my father (v. 8) — and then asks God to keep his word: let your word to David my father be now fulfilled (v. 9). What he wants is wisdom and knowledge to go out and come in before this people, for who can govern this people of yours, which is so great? (v. 10). God answers by listing what was not asked for — possessions, wealth, honour, the life of his enemies, long life — and grants the wisdom and adds the rest (vv. 11-12). Solomon comes back to Jerusalem and reigns (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: He asks God to do what God has already promised, which is how his father prayed after Nathan brought him the covenant. Neither of them invents a request. They take what God has said and hand it back to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice the pronoun in verse 10. Not this people of mine, on the throne God has just given him — this people of yours. He is asking for the competence to look after somebody else's property.

verseByVerse.quote: In that night God appeared to Solomon, and said to him, "Ask what I shall give you." And Solomon said to God, "You have shown great and steadfast love to David my father, and have made me king in his place. O LORD God, let your word to David my father be now fulfilled, for you have made me king over a people as numerous as the dust of the earth. Give me now wisdom and knowledge to go out and come in before this people, for who can govern this people of yours, which is so great?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that night God appeared to Solomon, and said to him, Ask what I shall give you.

An open question, with nothing ruled out. It is the most exposing thing that can happen to a person, because the answer is not a decision so much as a disclosure: whatever comes out was already there. Solomon does not get time to prepare it.

And he does not begin with himself. You have shown great and steadfast love to David my father, and have made me king in his place. The first sentence out of him is about somebody else's history with God, and the word he reaches for is the covenant word — the steadfast love the choir at the ark had sung endures forever.

Then the request, and it is anchored to a promise. O LORD God, let your word to David my father be now fulfilled. That is precisely how his father had prayed on the night the covenant was given: do as you have spoken. Neither of them asks God for something new. They find what he has already said and hand it back to him as a petition, and a boy who learned to pray that way learned it in that house.

And what he asks for is not what a king wants. Give me now wisdom and knowledge to go out and come in before this people. Going out and coming in before people is the old phrase for leading a flock; it is what Moses asked God to provide when he wanted a successor so that Israel would not be as sheep without a shepherd, and it is what the elders said David had been doing under Saul.

Then the reason, and it turns on one pronoun. For who can govern this people of yours, which is so great? Not my people. He has been on the throne a matter of months and he has already worked out that the nation is not his, and that he is asking for the competence to look after what belongs to somebody else.

verseByVerse.quote: God answered Solomon, "Because this was in your heart, and you have not asked for possessions, wealth, honor, or the life of those who hate you, and have not even asked for long life, but have asked for wisdom and knowledge for yourself that you may govern my people over whom I have made you king, wisdom and knowledge are granted to you. I will also give you riches, possessions, and honor, such as none of the kings had who were before you, and none after you shall have the like." So Solomon came from the high place at Gibeon, from before the tent of meeting, to Jerusalem. And he reigned over Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's answer begins by naming what was not said.

Because this was in your heart, and you have not asked for possessions, wealth, honor, or the life of those who hate you, and have not even asked for long life ...

Five things, itemised. Money, property, reputation, the death of his enemies, and a long life. Every one of them is what a new king in that world would have asked for, and God has evidently been listening for them. The commendation is not that Solomon asked for something noble but that he did not ask for those five, and God says so before he says anything else.

And the opening clause treats the request as evidence rather than as an achievement — because this was in your heart. God is not rewarding a clever answer. He is reading one.

Then the grant. Wisdom and knowledge are granted to you. I will also give you riches, possessions, and honor, such as none of the kings had who were before you, and none after you shall have the like. He gets what he asked for, and three of the five things he did not ask for arrive with it.

The account in Kings has one more clause at this point, and it is missing here: a condition, that if Solomon would walk in God's ways and keep his statutes, his days would be lengthened. Chronicles leaves the condition out and prints only the gift. Hold that in mind for four verses, because the chapter is about to show what Solomon did with the riches.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes on an inventory. Solomon gathers 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen and quarters them in the chariot cities and at Jerusalem (v. 14); silver and gold become as common in Jerusalem as stone and cedar as plentiful as the sycamores of the lowland (v. 15). And the supply line is named: Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt and Kue, at 600 shekels a chariot and 150 a horse, with a resale trade to the Hittite and Syrian kings (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Read one way this is verse 12 coming true in front of the reader: the riches and honour God promised, arriving. Read another way it is the law of the king being broken in the same breath — Deuteronomy forbade the king to accumulate horses, and named Egypt as the place he was not to get them from. The Chronicler sets it down and offers no verdict at all.
verseByVerse.examples: His father captured chariot horses and crippled them rather than build a chariot corps, because of that same law. The son bought fourteen hundred and set up a dealership.

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem. And the king made silver and gold as common in Jerusalem as stone, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah. And Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt and Kue, and the king's traders would buy them from Kue for a price. They imported a chariot from Egypt for 600 shekels of silver, and a horse for 150. Likewise through them these were exported to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Syria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with an inventory, and it is not as simple as it looks.

Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen. Silver and gold become as common in Jerusalem as stone; cedar is as plentiful as the scrubby sycamores of the coastal lowland. On one reading this is verse 12 arriving on schedule. God said riches and honour, and here they are, in figures.

Then verse 16 names the supplier. Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt and Kue.

Now open Deuteronomy at the law of the king. He shall not multiply horses to himself, it says, nor cause the people to return to Egypt in order to multiply horses. Two prohibitions in one sentence, and the chapter has just broken both of them in the same breath — many horses, and Egypt named as the source.

His father had faced the identical question and answered it the other way. When David captured a thousand chariots from Hadadezer he hamstrung the horses and kept enough for a hundred, crippling the most valuable military asset in the region rather than build the sort of army that teaches a nation to trust its own hardware. The son bought fourteen hundred and set up a resale business selling them on to the Hittite and Syrian kings.

The Chronicler does not say a word about it. He reports the wealth as the promise kept, which it is, and he reports the source, which is the one place the law had forbidden, and he leaves the two facts lying side by side on the page. Both are true. Solomon's gold and his wisdom came from God, and the first thing he did with them was start an arms trade with Egypt, and four hundred years later this book will end with Judah going back to Egypt for help one last time before Babylon takes the city.

2.title: Who Am I to Build a House?
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Solomon purposed to build a temple for the name of the LORD, and a royal palace for himself.<sup>2</sup>And Solomon assigned 70,000 men to bear burdens and 80,000 to quarry in the hill country, and 3,600 to oversee them.<sup>3</sup>And Solomon sent word to Hiram the king of Tyre: "As you dealt with David my father and sent him cedar to build himself a house to dwell in, so deal with me.<sup>4</sup>Behold, I am about to build a house for the name of the LORD my God and dedicate it to him for the burning of incense of sweet spices before him, and for the regular arrangement of the showbread, and for burnt offerings morning and evening, on the Sabbaths and the new moons and the appointed feasts of the LORD our God, as ordained forever for Israel.<sup>5</sup>The house that I am to build will be great, for our God is greater than all gods.<sup>6</sup>But who is able to build him a house, since heaven, even highest heaven, cannot contain him? Who am I to build a house for him, except as a place to make offerings before him?<sup>7</sup>So now send me a man skilled to work in gold, silver, bronze, and iron, and in purple, crimson, and blue fabrics, trained also in engraving, to be with the skilled workers who are with me in Judah and Jerusalem, whom David my father provided.<sup>8</sup>Send me also cedar, cypress, and algum timber from Lebanon, for I know that your servants know how to cut timber in Lebanon. And my servants will be with your servants,<sup>9</sup>to prepare timber for me in abundance, for the house I am to build will be great and wonderful.<sup>10</sup>I will give for your servants, the woodsmen who cut timber, 20,000 cors of crushed wheat, 20,000 cors of barley, 20,000 baths of wine, and 20,000 baths of oil."<sup>11</sup>Then Hiram the king of Tyre answered in a letter that he sent to Solomon, "Because the LORD loves his people, he has made you king over them."<sup>12</sup>Hiram also said, "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, who made heaven and earth, who has given King David a wise son, who has discretion and understanding, who will build a temple for the LORD and a royal palace for himself.<sup>13</sup>"Now I have sent a skilled man, who has understanding, Huram-abi,<sup>14</sup>the son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, and his father was a man of Tyre. He is trained to work in gold, silver, bronze, iron, stone, and wood, and in purple, blue, and crimson fabrics and fine linen, and to do all sorts of engraving and execute any design that may be assigned him, with your craftsmen, the craftsmen of my lord, David your father.<sup>15</sup>Now therefore the wheat and barley, oil and wine, of which my lord has spoken, let him send to his servants.<sup>16</sup>And we will cut whatever timber you need from Lebanon and bring it to you in rafts by sea to Joppa, so that you may take it up to Jerusalem."<sup>17</sup>Then Solomon counted all the resident aliens who were in the land of Israel, after the census of them that David his father had taken, and there were found 153,600.<sup>18</sup>Seventy thousand of them he assigned to bear burdens, 80,000 to quarry in the hill country, and 3,600 as overseers to make the people work.
2.overview:
Solomon sets out to build a temple and a palace and puts 153,600 men to work (vv. 1-2). His letter to Hiram of Tyre names what the house is for — incense, showbread, the offerings morning and evening — and states the paradox that governs the whole project: no house can contain the God it is built for (vv. 3-6). He asks for a master craftsman, for Lebanese timber, and names the woodsmen's wages (vv. 7-10). Hiram replies blessing the LORD as maker of heaven and earth, and sends Huram-abi, whose mother was of Dan and whose father was of Tyre (vv. 11-16). The labour is then identified: the resident aliens, counted from David's own register (vv. 17-18).

The two figures at either end of the chapter balance exactly, and the man Hiram sends is described in the words Exodus used of the craftsman who built the tabernacle.
2.theology:
Verses 5 and 6 settle what a temple is before one is built. The house will be great because God is greater than all gods — and in the same breath, no house can hold him, and neither can the highest heaven. So it is not a dwelling. It is a place to make offerings before him: somewhere a nation can bring blood and bread and know it has been received. Solomon will say the same thing again on the day the building is dedicated.

And a foreign king states the doctrine of Israel's monarchy better than most Israelites did: because the LORD loves his people, he has made you king over them. The throne exists for the sake of the people, and the people because God loves them — which is what the Chronicler wrote of David the first time cedar came from this same city.
2.examples:
Solomon told Hiram plainly that the Phoenicians knew how to cut timber and his own people did not. He had been given wisdom a fortnight earlier, and one of the first things it produced was the ability to say that somebody else was better at something.

He specified the wages for the woodsmen — wheat, barley, wine and oil, by the twenty thousand — in the same letter that ordered the timber, before anybody asked. The men doing the felling were named as the recipients.

The house was commissioned for bread set out, incense burned, and sacrifices at the same hours every morning and evening. The most expensive building in the nation's history existed to make a routine possible.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon sets out to build two things at once — a temple for the name of the LORD, and a royal palace for himself (v. 1) — and puts 153,600 men on the work (v. 2). Then he writes to Hiram of Tyre, asking for the same dealing his father had (v. 3) and naming what the house is for: incense, showbread, and the burnt offerings morning and evening on Sabbaths and new moons and feasts (v. 4). The letter then says the thing the whole project has to live with — who is able to build him a house, since heaven, even highest heaven, cannot contain him? (vv. 5-6) — before asking for a master craftsman, for timber, and naming the wages he will pay the woodsmen (vv. 7-10).
verseByVerse.theology: He states the paradox before a stone is laid. The house will be great because God is greater than all gods, and no house can hold him, and therefore it is not a residence at all but a place to make offerings before him. Solomon has defined the building correctly in the letter that commissions the timber.
verseByVerse.examples: The list in verse 4 is entirely ordinary — bread set out, incense burned, sacrifices morning and evening, the feasts as they come round. The most magnificent building in Israel's history was commissioned to house a routine.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Solomon purposed to build a temple for the name of the LORD, and a royal palace for himself. And Solomon assigned 70,000 men to bear burdens and 80,000 to quarry in the hill country, and 3,600 to oversee them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Solomon purposed to build a temple for the name of the LORD, and a royal palace for himself.

Both, in one sentence, with no comment on either. The account in Kings supplies the figures that make the pairing uncomfortable: seven years on the house of the LORD and thirteen on his own. Chronicles is not interested in the palace and will mention it once more in passing, but it lets the two projects stand side by side in the opening line, and a reader is free to notice which one took longer.

Then the labour force. Seventy thousand to carry, eighty thousand to quarry in the hill country, three thousand six hundred to supervise. That is a hundred and fifty-three thousand six hundred men, and the figure comes back exactly at the end of the chapter, where the Chronicler says who they were.

Stop on the scale for a moment. Israel had never done anything like this. A nation that had been a confederation of tribes with no capital two generations earlier now has a standing workforce larger than most of the armies in the region, cutting stone.

verseByVerse.quote: And Solomon sent word to Hiram the king of Tyre: "As you dealt with David my father and sent him cedar to build himself a house to dwell in, so deal with me. Behold, I am about to build a house for the name of the LORD my God and dedicate it to him for the burning of incense of sweet spices before him, and for the regular arrangement of the showbread, and for burnt offerings morning and evening, on the Sabbaths and the new moons and the appointed feasts of the LORD our God, as ordained forever for Israel. The house that I am to build will be great, for our God is greater than all gods. But who is able to build him a house, since heaven, even highest heaven, cannot contain him? Who am I to build a house for him, except as a place to make offerings before him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letter to Tyre opens by invoking a relationship Solomon inherited. As you dealt with David my father and sent him cedar to build himself a house to dwell in, so deal with me. Hiram had sent cedar and masons to Jerusalem once before, and the son is trading on his father's account.

Then he says what the house is for, and the list is startlingly plain: incense of sweet spices, the regular arrangement of the showbread, burnt offerings morning and evening, on the Sabbaths and the new moons and the appointed feasts — as ordained forever for Israel. Not a monument, not a treasury, not a national symbol. A place where bread is set out and a fire is kept going and the same things happen at the same hours.

And then the two sentences that keep the whole enterprise honest.

The house that I am to build will be great, for our God is greater than all gods. But who is able to build him a house, since heaven, even highest heaven, cannot contain him? Who am I to build a house for him, except as a place to make offerings before him?

The greatness of the building is argued from the greatness of God, and then in the very next breath the argument is turned round on itself. If he is that great, no building can hold him — and the highest heaven cannot either, which disposes of the idea that God is merely somewhere else. So what is the house? Not a residence. A place to make offerings before him: an address where a nation can bring blood and bread and know it has been received.

He says all this in a commercial letter ordering timber, before a stone has been cut. And the phrase in the middle of it — who am I — is the one his father used sitting in front of the ark when the covenant was given, and used again in his last prayer with the gold heaped in the courtyard. It has evidently been said in that family more than once.

verseByVerse.quote: So now send me a man skilled to work in gold, silver, bronze, and iron, and in purple, crimson, and blue fabrics, trained also in engraving, to be with the skilled workers who are with me in Judah and Jerusalem, whom David my father provided. Send me also cedar, cypress, and algum timber from Lebanon, for I know that your servants know how to cut timber in Lebanon. And my servants will be with your servants, to prepare timber for me in abundance, for the house I am to build will be great and wonderful. I will give for your servants, the woodsmen who cut timber, 20,000 cors of crushed wheat, 20,000 cors of barley, 20,000 baths of wine, and 20,000 baths of oil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The request itself is specific. Not labourers — Solomon has a hundred and fifty thousand of those. He wants a man skilled to work in gold, silver, bronze, and iron, and in purple, crimson, and blue fabrics, trained also in engraving, to work alongside the craftsmen David had already gathered.

Then timber, and a reason: for I know that your servants know how to cut timber in Lebanon. It is a straightforward admission that the Phoenicians were better at something than the Israelites were, made by a king who has just been told he is the wisest man alive. Wisdom is quite compatible with hiring people who can do what you cannot.

And he names the wages before he is asked: twenty thousand cors of crushed wheat, twenty thousand of barley, twenty thousand baths of wine and twenty thousand of oil, specified as payment for your servants, the woodsmen who cut timber. Not a lump sum to the king of Tyre — provisions for the men doing the felling.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — Hiram's Answer, and the Craftsman
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hiram replies in writing, and blesses Israel's God: Because the LORD loves his people, he has made you king over them (v. 11), and Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, who made heaven and earth (v. 12). He sends Huram-abi, whose mother was of the daughters of Dan and whose father was a man of Tyre, trained in gold, silver, bronze, iron, stone and wood, in purple and blue and crimson and fine linen, in engraving, and able to execute any design that may be assigned him (vv. 13-14). The timber will come down the coast in rafts to Joppa (vv. 15-16). And the labour is counted: 153,600 resident aliens (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: A Phoenician king writes that the LORD made heaven and earth, and that Solomon is on the throne because God loves the people — which is exactly what the Chronicler said about David and the cedar. It may be no more than good diplomacy. The Chronicler prints it and passes no verdict.
verseByVerse.examples: Huram-abi's list of skills is the list given of Bezalel at Sinai, almost item for item, and his mother's tribe is the tribe of the man God appointed to work beside Bezalel. The temple is being built by the tabernacle's kind of craftsman.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Hiram the king of Tyre answered in a letter that he sent to Solomon, "Because the LORD loves his people, he has made you king over them." Hiram also said, "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, who made heaven and earth, who has given King David a wise son, who has discretion and understanding, who will build a temple for the LORD and a royal palace for himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hiram writes back, and the first sentence of his reply is not about cedar.

Because the LORD loves his people, he has made you king over them.

A Phoenician monarch, whose city worshipped Melqart and whose granddaughter would be Jezebel, gives the reason for Solomon's throne — and gets it right. The king is on the throne for the sake of the people, because God loves them. That is precisely what the Chronicler said when Hiram's cedar first arrived in David's Jerusalem: the kingdom was highly exalted for the sake of his people Israel. The foreigner has read the arrangement correctly.

Then: Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, who made heaven and earth, who has given King David a wise son. A blessing pronounced on the LORD by name, and the LORD identified as maker of heaven and earth — not one god among the region's many, but the one.

How much Hiram meant of it cannot be known, and courtesy between courts was an art with conventions of its own. The Chronicler prints the letter and adds nothing. His own readers lived under a Persian administration and had every reason to notice that a foreign king had once put that sentence in writing about their God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now I have sent a skilled man, who has understanding, Huram-abi, the son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, and his father was a man of Tyre. He is trained to work in gold, silver, bronze, iron, stone, and wood, and in purple, blue, and crimson fabrics and fine linen, and to do all sorts of engraving and execute any design that may be assigned him, with your craftsmen, the craftsmen of my lord, David your father. Now therefore the wheat and barley, oil and wine, of which my lord has spoken, let him send to his servants. And we will cut whatever timber you need from Lebanon and bring it to you in rafts by sea to Joppa, so that you may take it up to Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man Hiram sends is described at more length than anyone else in the chapter.

Huram-abi, the son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, and his father was a man of Tyre. Half Israelite and half Phoenician, and the temple's master craftsman.

Then his skills: gold, silver, bronze, iron, stone, wood; purple, blue and crimson fabrics and fine linen; engraving; and the capacity to execute any design that may be assigned him. Set that beside the description of the man God named to Moses at Sinai — Bezalel, filled with the Spirit of God to devise artistic designs, to work in gold and silver and bronze, in cutting stones and carving wood, and, with Oholiab, in engraving and in weaving blue and purple and scarlet and fine twined linen. It is the same list.

And there is a detail in the parentage that may not be an accident. Oholiab, the man God appointed to stand beside Bezalel, was of the tribe of Dan. The temple's craftsman has a Danite mother. The Chronicler describes the second builder in the terms of the first, and the reader who knows Exodus is meant to hear it.

One honest difficulty: the account in Kings says Huram-abi's mother was a widow of the tribe of Naphtali. Chronicles says Dan. The two cannot both be pressed at once, and the usual suggestions — a Danite woman who had married into Naphtali, or a widow of a Naphtalite man — are guesses. Nobody can settle it, and nothing in the chapter turns on it.

The timber comes by sea, lashed into rafts and floated down the coast to Joppa, then hauled thirty-five miles uphill to Jerusalem. Every cedar beam in that building was dragged up from the coastal plain by hand.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon counted all the resident aliens who were in the land of Israel, after the census of them that David his father had taken, and there were found 153,600. Seventy thousand of them he assigned to bear burdens, 80,000 to quarry in the hill country, and 3,600 as overseers to make the people work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends by saying who the hundred and fifty-three thousand were.

Then Solomon counted all the resident aliens who were in the land of Israel, after the census of them that David his father had taken, and there were found 153,600.

The figure balances the one in verse 2 exactly — seventy thousand carriers, eighty thousand quarrymen, three thousand six hundred overseers. And the men are the gerim, the foreigners settled in the land, counted from a register David had already drawn up when he set them to cutting stone for a building he would never see.

It was conscription, and the Chronicler does not dress it up. He does make one distinction, and he will state it plainly in chapter 8: of the people of Israel, Solomon made no slaves for his work. The burden fell on the residents who were not Israelites, and the book says so in figures rather than defending it.

So the stones of the house were squared by men who would not be allowed past its outer court. The building they cut them for was one a later prophet would hear God call a house of prayer for all peoples, and the foreigner who joined himself to the LORD was promised a name inside those walls better than sons and daughters.

3.title: He Began to Build
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to David his father, at the place that David had appointed, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.<sup>2</sup>He began to build in the second month of the fourth year of his reign.<sup>3</sup>These are Solomon's measurements for building the house of God: the length, in cubits of the old standard, was sixty cubits, and the breadth twenty cubits.<sup>4</sup>The vestibule in front of the nave of the house was twenty cubits long, equal to the width of the house, and its height was 120 cubits. He overlaid it on the inside with pure gold.<sup>5</sup>The nave he lined with cypress and covered it with fine gold and made palms and chains on it.<sup>6</sup>He adorned the house with settings of precious stones. The gold was gold of Parvaim.<sup>7</sup>So he lined the house with gold—its beams, its thresholds, its walls, and its doors— and he carved cherubim on the walls.<sup>8</sup>And he made the Most Holy Place. Its length, corresponding to the breadth of the house, was twenty cubits, and its breadth was twenty cubits. He overlaid it with 600 talents of fine gold.<sup>9</sup>The weight of gold for the nails was fifty shekels. And he overlaid the upper chambers with gold.<sup>10</sup>In the Most Holy Place he made two cherubim of wood and overlaid them with gold.<sup>11</sup>The wings of the cherubim together extended twenty cubits: one wing of the one, of five cubits, touched the wall of the house, and its other wing, of five cubits, touched the wing of the other cherub;<sup>12</sup>and of this cherub, one wing, of five cubits, touched the wall of the house, and the other wing, also of five cubits, was joined to the wing of the first cherub.<sup>13</sup>The wings of these cherubim extended twenty cubits. The cherubim stood on their feet, facing the nave.<sup>14</sup>And he made the veil of blue and purple and crimson fabrics and fine linen, and he worked cherubim on it.<sup>15</sup>In front of the house he made two pillars thirty-five cubits high, with a capital of five cubits on the top of each.<sup>16</sup>He made chains like a necklace and put them on the tops of the pillars, and he made a hundred pomegranates and put them on the chains.<sup>17</sup>He set up the pillars in front of the temple, one on the south, the other on the north; that on the south he called Jachin, and that on the north Boaz.
3.overview:
The building begins, and the first verse locates it three times over: on Mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared to David, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite (v. 1). The measurements follow in cubits of the old standard, with gold over the beams and walls and doors and six hundred talents on the Most Holy Place — and fifty shekels of gold for the nails (vv. 2-9). Two cherubim span the inner room wall to wall and stand facing outward (vv. 10-13); the veil is made to the tabernacle's own specification (v. 14); and two free-standing pillars are set at the door and named Jachin and Boaz (vv. 15-17).

Only this book calls the temple mount Moriah. It is where Abraham was sent with his son, and where the angel's sword stopped over Jerusalem.
3.theology:
Verse 1 ties three events into one piece of ground. A father climbed that hill with his son and a knife and came down with a ram provided in his son's place. A king stood on it while an angel held a drawn sword over the city, and offered on an altar God lit himself. And a farmer sold it for its full price to a man who would not bring God an offering that cost him nothing. Substitution, judgement halted, and a price paid — and the altar of Israel stood on all three.

Inside, the cherubim have changed posture. The pair over the mercy seat looked down at the blood; these stand on their feet and face outward into the room. And the veil in front of them carries the same embroidered guardians that hung in the wilderness — the reminder, renewed in gold and fine linen, that the way in was still shut. It stayed shut until it was torn.
3.examples:
The nails were gilded. Fifty shekels of gold went on the fixings, which nobody would ever look at, in a building whose visible surfaces were already covered. The father had gathered the iron for them and the son weighed out gold.

The two pillars hold nothing up. They exist to be walked between and to be read: he will establish, and in him is strength. Israel put its doctrine at the door in bronze rather than on a wall in words.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to David his father, at the place that David had appointed, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite (v. 1). The date is the second month of the fourth year (v. 2). Then the measurements, given in cubits of the old standard — sixty by twenty, with the vestibule across the front (vv. 3-4) — and the gold: the nave lined with cypress and covered with fine gold, palms and chains and settings of precious stones (vv. 5-7), six hundred talents on the Most Holy Place, and the weight of gold for the nails was fifty shekels (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: One verse ties three things together that stand five hundred years apart: the hill where Abraham was sent to offer his son and found a ram caught in a thicket, the spot where the angel's sword stopped and fire fell on a hurried altar, and a Jebusite farmer's threshing floor bought at full price. The temple stands on all three at once.
verseByVerse.examples: The nails were weighed in gold. David had stockpiled iron for the nails of the doors and the clamps; his son gilded them. There is no line in that house below which the care stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to David his father, at the place that David had appointed, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. He began to build in the second month of the fourth year of his reign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to David his father, at the place that David had appointed, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.

Everything the previous book was working towards is packed into that one sentence, and it identifies the ground three separate times.

Mount Moriah. That name has been used once before in Scripture, when a man was told to take his only son to the land of Moriah and offer him on one of the mountains there, and walked three days to do it, and lifted the knife, and was stopped by a voice, and looked up and saw a ram caught by its horns in a thicket. No other book in the Bible calls the temple mount by that name. This one does, in the first line of the building account.

Where the LORD had appeared to David his father. That is the angel standing between earth and heaven with a drawn sword over the city, and the fire that came down on an altar built in a hurry while seventy thousand people were being buried.

On the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. A working farm on the high ground, with wheat still lying on it, bought for six hundred shekels of gold by a king who would not offer God anything that had cost him nothing.

A substitute provided, a judgement halted, a price paid in full. The house went up on top of all three, and every sacrifice offered there for the next four hundred years was offered on that hill.

The date is given as the second month of the fourth year of the reign. The account in Kings adds another figure — the four hundred and eightieth year after Israel came out of Egypt — and Chronicles leaves it out, as it leaves out most of what does not bear on the house itself.

verseByVerse.quote: These are Solomon's measurements for building the house of God: the length, in cubits of the old standard, was sixty cubits, and the breadth twenty cubits. The vestibule in front of the nave of the house was twenty cubits long, equal to the width of the house, and its height was 120 cubits. He overlaid it on the inside with pure gold. The nave he lined with cypress and covered it with fine gold and made palms and chains on it. He adorned the house with settings of precious stones. The gold was gold of Parvaim. So he lined the house with gold—its beams, its thresholds, its walls, and its doors— and he carved cherubim on the walls. And he made the Most Holy Place. Its length, corresponding to the breadth of the house, was twenty cubits, and its breadth was twenty cubits. He overlaid it with 600 talents of fine gold. The weight of gold for the nails was fifty shekels. And he overlaid the upper chambers with gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the measurements, and a small honest note attached to them: the length and breadth are given in cubits of the old standard. The measure had changed between the building and the writing, and the Chronicler tells his readers which one he is using. He is working from records made a long time before, for people who would otherwise get the building wrong in their heads.

Sixty cubits by twenty — about ninety feet by thirty, which is not large. The tent it replaced was half those dimensions. What is extraordinary is not the footprint but what went onto the surfaces: cypress lining, fine gold over the beams and thresholds and walls and doors, carved palms and chains, settings of precious stones, six hundred talents of gold on the Most Holy Place alone.

The vestibule is given a height of a hundred and twenty cubits, which would be a tower three times as long as the house is deep, and the account in Kings gives the building thirty cubits. The figure has been discussed for a very long time and the honest position is that nobody can account for it with confidence.

And then, in the middle of the talents: The weight of gold for the nails was fifty shekels. His father had laid up great quantities of iron for nails, for the doors of the gates and for the clamps, in his last years, for a building he would never enter. The son gilded them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Cherubim, Veil, and Two Pillars
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two cherubim of wood overlaid with gold are made for the Most Holy Place, their wings spanning the full twenty cubits from wall to wall (vv. 10-12), and they stood on their feet, facing the nave (v. 13). Then the veil — blue and purple and crimson and fine linen, and he worked cherubim on it (v. 14). And in front of the house two pillars with capitals, chains like a necklace and a hundred pomegranates, set one to the south and one to the north and given names: that on the south he called Jachin, and that on the north Boaz (vv. 15-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The tabernacle's cherubim faced each other and looked down at the mercy seat. These stand up and face outward, into the room where the priests worked. What guarded the way in is now looking out at the people.
verseByVerse.examples: The two pillars carry no roof. They stand free in front of the porch holding nothing up, and their names make a sentence: he will establish, and in him is strength.

verseByVerse.quote: In the Most Holy Place he made two cherubim of wood and overlaid them with gold. The wings of the cherubim together extended twenty cubits: one wing of the one, of five cubits, touched the wall of the house, and its other wing, of five cubits, touched the wing of the other cherub; and of this cherub, one wing, of five cubits, touched the wall of the house, and the other wing, also of five cubits, was joined to the wing of the first cherub. The wings of these cherubim extended twenty cubits. The cherubim stood on their feet, facing the nave. And he made the veil of blue and purple and crimson fabrics and fine linen, and he worked cherubim on it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two cherubim are made for the innermost room, carved in wood and covered with gold, and the arithmetic of their wings is given twice over: five cubits touching the wall, five cubits touching the wing of the other, on each side, so that the pair reach the full twenty cubits from one wall to the other. There is no space left in the room that is not under a wing.

Then a detail no other account gives. The cherubim stood on their feet, facing the nave.

The two on the mercy seat in the wilderness faced each other with their faces turned down, looking at the place where the blood was put. These stand upright and look outward — through the doorway, into the room where the priests trimmed the lamps and set out the bread. The creatures that were posted at Eden with a flaming sword to keep the way are here standing at ease, facing the congregation.

And then the veil, which Chronicles alone mentions in this building: blue and purple and crimson fabrics and fine linen, and he worked cherubim on it. That is the specification of the tabernacle curtain, item for item, given to Moses at Sinai. Four hundred years on, the same four colours and the same embroidered guardians hang between the people and the room they may not enter.

It hung there, or its successor did, until a Friday afternoon when the earth shook and it was torn from the top to the bottom, and the way the cherubim had been guarding since Eden was open.

verseByVerse.quote: In front of the house he made two pillars thirty-five cubits high, with a capital of five cubits on the top of each. He made chains like a necklace and put them on the tops of the pillars, and he made a hundred pomegranates and put them on the chains. He set up the pillars in front of the temple, one on the south, the other on the north; that on the south he called Jachin, and that on the north Boaz.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two pillars are set up in front of the house, thirty-five cubits high with capitals of five cubits, hung with chains like a necklace and a hundred pomegranates. The account in Kings gives eighteen cubits apiece, and the usual explanation is that Chronicles has given the pair as one measurement; it cannot be proved.

What matters is what they were doing there, which is nothing. They stand free, in front of the porch, carrying no roof and supporting no wall. They are not architecture. They are a statement, planted where every worshipper had to walk between them.

And they were named. That on the south he called Jachin, and that on the north Boaz. The names are sentences: he will establish, and in him is strength. Say them together and they are the whole doctrine of the covenant standing in bronze at the door — not that the house is strong, or the king, or the nation, but that he establishes and the strength is his.

Three and a half centuries later the Babylonians broke both pillars in pieces and carried the bronze to Babylon. The sentence they spelled outlasted them.

4.title: The Bronze Sea and the Golden Lampstands
4.text: <sup>1</sup>He made an altar of bronze, twenty cubits long and twenty cubits wide and ten cubits high.<sup>2</sup>Then he made the sea of cast metal. It was round, ten cubits from brim to brim, and five cubits high, and a line of thirty cubits measured its circumference.<sup>3</sup>Under it were figures of gourds, for ten cubits, compassing the sea all around. The gourds were in two rows, cast with it when it was cast.<sup>4</sup>It stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east. The sea was set on them, and all their rear parts were inward.<sup>5</sup>Its thickness was a handbreadth. And its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It held 3,000 baths.<sup>6</sup>He also made ten basins in which to wash, and set five on the south side, and five on the north side. In these they were to rinse off what was used for the burnt offering, and the sea was for the priests to wash in.<sup>7</sup>And he made ten golden lampstands as prescribed, and set them in the temple, five on the south side and five on the north.<sup>8</sup>He also made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the south side and five on the north. And he made a hundred basins of gold.<sup>9</sup>He made the court of the priests and the great court and doors for the court and overlaid their doors with bronze.<sup>10</sup>And he set the sea at the southeast corner of the house.<sup>11</sup>Hiram also made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. So Hiram finished the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of God:<sup>12</sup>the two pillars, the bowls, and the two capitals on the top of the pillars; and the two latticeworks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the top of the pillars;<sup>13</sup>and the 400 pomegranates for the two latticeworks, two rows of pomegranates for each latticework, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the pillars.<sup>14</sup>He made the stands also, and the basins on the stands,<sup>15</sup>and the one sea, and the twelve oxen underneath it.<sup>16</sup>The pots, the shovels, the forks, and all the equipment for these Huram-abi made of burnished bronze for King Solomon for the house of the LORD.<sup>17</sup>In the plain of the Jordan the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredah.<sup>18</sup>Solomon made all these things in great quantities, for the weight of the bronze was not sought.<sup>19</sup>So Solomon made all the vessels that were in the house of God: the golden altar, the tables for the bread of the Presence,<sup>20</sup>the lampstands and their lamps of pure gold to burn before the inner sanctuary, as prescribed;<sup>21</sup>the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs, of purest gold;<sup>22</sup>the snuffers, basins, dishes for incense, and fire pans, of pure gold, and the sockets of the temple, for the inner doors to the Most Holy Place and for the doors of the nave of the temple were of gold.
4.overview:
A bronze altar thirty feet square, and the sea — cast in one piece on twelve oxen facing the four directions, its brim flared like a lily (vv. 1-5). Ten basins rinse what is offered; the sea is for the priests themselves to wash in (v. 6). Ten lampstands and ten tables where the tabernacle had one of each, a hundred gold basins, and two courts with bronze doors (vv. 7-10). Huram-abi's bronze work is totalled and its foundry named — the clay ground in the Jordan plain — and there was so much of it that nobody weighed it (vv. 11-18). The gold vessels close the chapter, down to the snuffers and the door sockets (vv. 19-22).

Only Chronicles records the bronze altar. And the bronze the sea was cast from was captured in a Syrian war a generation before the building existed.
4.theology:
Verse 6 makes a division the whole sacrificial system depends on. The basins rinse the offering; the sea washes the men who bring it. Something clean can be carried by hands that are not, and the house was built with a far larger provision for the second problem than the first. The letter to the Hebrews tells Christians to draw near with hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed with pure water, and it is this basin behind the sentence.

And everything here is the tabernacle enlarged rather than replaced. One lampstand becomes ten, one table ten, and the phrase as prescribed is attached to hold the pattern in place. What Israel could finally afford it spent on doing exactly what it had been told to do in the wilderness, at scale.
4.examples:
The foundry was in the Jordan valley because that is where the clay is — thirty miles away and three thousand feet below the site. Everything cast there had to be hauled uphill afterwards. The work that makes a thing possible is usually done a long way from where the thing will stand.

The snuffers were pure gold, and so were the door sockets, which disappeared under the doors the day they were hung. Nobody was going to see them. They were made of gold because of whose house it was.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Altar, the Sea, and the Lampstands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A bronze altar thirty feet square and fifteen high (v. 1); then the sea, cast in one piece, ten cubits across and five deep, standing on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east, its brim flared like the flower of a lily, holding three thousand baths (vv. 2-5). Ten basins are set five to a side to rinse what is offered, and the sea was for the priests to wash in (v. 6). Ten golden lampstands and ten tables follow, five south and five north, with a hundred golden basins (vv. 7-8); then the court of the priests, the great court, and doors overlaid with bronze (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 6 divides the washing in two. The basins rinse what is going onto the altar; the sea is for the men who put it there. The offering has to be clean and so does the one who brings it, and the second is the harder of the two.
verseByVerse.examples: The tabernacle had one lampstand and one table. This house has ten of each, and a hundred gold basins. Everything Moses made in single copies has been multiplied by a nation that could finally afford it.

verseByVerse.quote: He made an altar of bronze, twenty cubits long and twenty cubits wide and ten cubits high. Then he made the sea of cast metal. It was round, ten cubits from brim to brim, and five cubits high, and a line of thirty cubits measured its circumference. Under it were figures of gourds, for ten cubits, compassing the sea all around. The gourds were in two rows, cast with it when it was cast. It stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east. The sea was set on them, and all their rear parts were inward. Its thickness was a handbreadth. And its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It held 3,000 baths. He also made ten basins in which to wash, and set five on the south side, and five on the north side. In these they were to rinse off what was used for the burnt offering, and the sea was for the priests to wash in.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The altar comes first, and it is enormous: twenty cubits by twenty by ten, which is thirty feet square and fifteen high. A man could not reach the top of it. The account in Kings never records its making at all; only this book gives the dimensions.

Set it beside the altar Solomon was sacrificing on three chapters ago. Bezalel's bronze altar, made in the wilderness, was five cubits square and three high. The new one has sixteen times the surface. Everything about this house is the old pattern enlarged.

Then the sea. Cast in one piece, ten cubits from brim to brim and five deep, thirty cubits round, a handbreadth thick, with two rows of gourds cast into it and a brim that flared out like the flower of a lily. It held three thousand baths — the account in Kings says two thousand, and the difference has never been resolved. Thirty round to ten across is a round number for a round object in a text that is not doing geometry, and the flared rim would account for the rest.

It stood on twelve bronze oxen, three facing each quarter of the compass, with their hindquarters inward. Twelve, for the tribes, holding up the water the priests washed in — and two centuries later a king of Judah called Ahaz will cut the sea down off them and take the oxen for himself.

And verse 6 separates two things that are easy to confuse. Ten basins are for rinsing what was used for the burnt offering — the carcass, the pieces going up. The sea is something else: the sea was for the priests to wash in.

The gift has to be clean and so does the man carrying it. It is possible to bring God something spotless with unwashed hands, and the house was built with a separate and much larger provision for the second problem. A later letter tells Christians to draw near with a true heart, their bodies washed with pure water, and it is this basin it has in view.

verseByVerse.quote: And he made ten golden lampstands as prescribed, and set them in the temple, five on the south side and five on the north. He also made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the south side and five on the north. And he made a hundred basins of gold. He made the court of the priests and the great court and doors for the court and overlaid their doors with bronze. And he set the sea at the southeast corner of the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ten golden lampstands, five on the south side and five on the north. Ten tables, five and five. A hundred basins of gold.

The tent in the wilderness had one lampstand and one table. Everything Moses was told to make in a single copy stands here ten times over, in a room lined with gold, in a nation that had spent four hundred years unable to afford any of it.

The multiplication is not extravagance for its own sake — the pattern is kept exactly, and the phrase as prescribed is attached to the lampstands to say so. What has changed is the scale, not the design.

Then the courts: one for the priests and a great court outside it, with doors overlaid in bronze. Two enclosures, one inside the other, and a gate between them. The building is being arranged in degrees of nearness, and everyone who used it knew exactly how far in they were allowed to go.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Huram-abi's work is then totalled: pots, shovels, basins; the two pillars with their bowls and capitals and latticework; the four hundred pomegranates; the stands and their basins; and the one sea, and the twelve oxen underneath it (vv. 11-16). The casting was done in the plain of the Jordan ... in the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredah (v. 17), and there was so much of it that the weight of the bronze was not sought (v. 18). The gold work closes the chapter: the golden altar, the tables for the bread of the Presence, the lampstands, tongs, snuffers, dishes and fire pans of pure gold, and even the door sockets (vv. 19-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The bronze in these verses was captured. David took it from two of Hadadezer's cities in a Syrian war a generation earlier, and the previous book says plainly that this is what became of it. The sea the priests washed in was melted down from somebody's war.
verseByVerse.examples: They stopped weighing it. David had weighed out the gold for every lamp and every fork and had already said the bronze was past weighing; his son's foundry proved him right.

verseByVerse.quote: Hiram also made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. So Hiram finished the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of God: the two pillars, the bowls, and the two capitals on the top of the pillars; and the two latticeworks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the top of the pillars; and the 400 pomegranates for the two latticeworks, two rows of pomegranates for each latticework, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the pillars. He made the stands also, and the basins on the stands, and the one sea, and the twelve oxen underneath it. The pots, the shovels, the forks, and all the equipment for these Huram-abi made of burnished bronze for King Solomon for the house of the LORD. In the plain of the Jordan the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredah. Solomon made all these things in great quantities, for the weight of the bronze was not sought.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Huram-abi's account is then closed off. So Hiram finished the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of God — and the list runs back over everything: the pots and shovels and basins, the two pillars with their bowls and capitals, the two latticeworks, the four hundred pomegranates, the stands and their basins, and the one sea, and the twelve oxen underneath it.

Where it was all made matters. In the plain of the Jordan the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredah. Casting bronze on that scale needs clay for the moulds, and the clay was down in the valley — so the foundry was thirty miles from the site and three thousand feet below it, and every piece had to be dragged up afterwards.

Then a sentence that says how much there was. Solomon made all these things in great quantities, for the weight of the bronze was not sought. Nobody weighed it. They gave up.

His father had weighed everything — gold by the item, for each lampstand and each lamp and each fork, written into the plan he handed over. And he had said, in the same breath, that the bronze and the iron were beyond weighing. The son's foundry is where that sentence was proved.

verseByVerse.quote: So Solomon made all the vessels that were in the house of God: the golden altar, the tables for the bread of the Presence, the lampstands and their lamps of pure gold to burn before the inner sanctuary, as prescribed; the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs, of purest gold; the snuffers, basins, dishes for incense, and fire pans, of pure gold, and the sockets of the temple, for the inner doors to the Most Holy Place and for the doors of the nave of the temple were of gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gold work finishes the chapter, and the list gets smaller as it goes. The golden altar and the tables for the bread of the Presence. The lampstands and their lamps of pure gold, to burn before the inner sanctuary, as prescribed. Then the flowers, the lamps and the tongs. Then the snuffers, the basins, the dishes for incense and the fire pans.

Snuffers. The little scissors for trimming a wick, made of pure gold, because they would be used in a room where God had said he would be. The plan David received had specified the weight of gold for the forks; his son had them made.

And the last item in the chapter is the least visible thing in the building: the sockets of the temple, for the inner doors to the Most Holy Place and for the doors of the nave of the temple were of gold. The hinges. Set into the floor and the frame, out of sight the moment the doors were hung, and made of gold because of where they were.

5.title: The Glory of the LORD Filled the House
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus all the work that Solomon did for the house of the LORD was finished. And Solomon brought in the things that David his father had dedicated, and stored the silver, the gold, and all the vessels in the treasuries of the house of God.<sup>2</sup>Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the leaders of the fathers' houses of the people of Israel, in Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of the city of David, which is Zion.<sup>3</sup>And all the men of Israel assembled before the king at the feast that is in the seventh month.<sup>4</sup>And all the elders of Israel came, and the Levites took up the ark.<sup>5</sup>And they brought up the ark, the tent of meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the tent; the Levitical priests brought them up.<sup>6</sup>And King Solomon and all the congregation of Israel, who had assembled before him, were before the ark, sacrificing so many sheep and oxen that they could not be counted or numbered.<sup>7</sup>Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place, in the inner sanctuary of the house, in the Most Holy Place, underneath the wings of the cherubim.<sup>8</sup>The cherubim spread out their wings over the place of the ark, so that the cherubim made a covering above the ark and its poles.<sup>9</sup>And the poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the Holy Place before the inner sanctuary, but they could not be seen from outside. And they are there to this day.<sup>10</sup>There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets that Moses put there at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel, when they came out of Egypt.<sup>11</sup>And when the priests came out of the Holy Place (for all the priests who were present had consecrated themselves, without regard to their divisions,<sup>12</sup>and all the Levitical singers, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, their sons and kinsmen, arrayed in fine linen, with cymbals, harps, and lyres, stood east of the altar with 120 priests who were trumpeters;<sup>13</sup>and it was the duty of the trumpeters and singers to make themselves heard in unison in praise and thanksgiving to the LORD), and when the song was raised, with trumpets and cymbals and other musical instruments, in praise to the LORD, "For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever," the house, the house of the LORD, was filled with a cloud,<sup>14</sup>so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of God.
5.overview:
The work is finished and David's dedicated silver and gold go into the treasuries (v. 1). Israel gathers at the feast of the seventh month, and the Levites carry the ark up from the city of David — bringing the tent of meeting and its vessels with it (vv. 2-6). The ark is set under the cherubim, the poles left in and visible from the Holy Place, and the reader is told what is inside: the two tablets and nothing else (vv. 7-10). Then every priest present, off-rota, and the singers with a hundred and twenty trumpeters; and when the song is raised the cloud fills the house so that the priests cannot stand (vv. 11-14).

Verse 5 closes a gap that has been open since 1 Chronicles 16. The tabernacle from Gibeon is carried in, and the two halves of Israel's worship are finally under one roof.
5.theology:
Verse 10 is the gospel laid out in furniture. Inside the ark is the law — the covenant Israel broke before Moses reached the bottom of the mountain and had gone on breaking for four centuries. Above it is a gold lid where blood was put once a year, and above that the wings. The commandments are not removed and not amended; they are covered, and the covering is blood. Romans takes the name of that lid and gives it to Christ, put forward publicly, in his blood.

And the cloud repeats what happened to Moses. When the tabernacle was finished the glory filled it and its builder could not go in; here the priests cannot stand. The Chronicler ties the song and the cloud together, and the song was six words about God's own goodness — not a technique, and not the singers' fervour. What is recorded is what happened when a nation did what it had been told, the way it had been told, with one voice.
5.examples:
The temple was dedicated during Tabernacles — the one week of the year when every Israelite left his house to live in a shelter of branches and remember that the nation once had no home. The people went into booths on the week God came indoors.

The poles were left in the rings, by a command given at Sinai, though the ark would never travel again. A priest in the Holy Place could see the ends of them pressing against the veil: the sign that the God now settled on that hill had spent four hundred years moving whenever his people moved.

For one day the twenty-four courses were suspended and every priest in the country served at once. A rota is what makes work last; there are days it cannot cope with, and somebody has to know which they are.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Thus all the work that Solomon did for the house of the LORD was finished, and David's dedicated silver and gold and vessels are brought in and stored (v. 1). Solomon assembles the elders and tribal heads to fetch the ark up out of the city of David (v. 2), and all Israel gathers at the feast that is in the seventh month (v. 3). The Levites took up the ark (v. 4) — and they bring up something else with it: the ark, the tent of meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the tent (v. 5). Sheep and oxen are sacrificed in numbers that could not be counted or numbered (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 5 closes a gap that has been open since the ark came to Jerusalem. The tabernacle Moses made has been standing at Gibeon with the altar in front of it while the ark sat in a tent on Zion, and now the old tent is carried in and the two halves of Israel's worship are in one building at last.
verseByVerse.examples: The Levites carried it. Nobody had to be told twice; the last time an ark moved without them a man died on a cart track, and the king who watched it happen spent three months finding out why.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus all the work that Solomon did for the house of the LORD was finished. And Solomon brought in the things that David his father had dedicated, and stored the silver, the gold, and all the vessels in the treasuries of the house of God. Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the leaders of the fathers' houses of the people of Israel, in Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of the city of David, which is Zion. And all the men of Israel assembled before the king at the feast that is in the seventh month.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus all the work that Solomon did for the house of the LORD was finished.

Seven years. And the first thing recorded after the last workman leaves is not an inspection or a ceremony but a delivery: Solomon brought in the things that David his father had dedicated, and stored the silver, the gold, and all the vessels in the treasuries of the house of God.

That is the pile. Everything taken from Edom and Moab and Ammon and Philistia and Amalek and set apart rather than spent; the gold of Ophir out of an old man's private fortune; and the dedicated gifts that had been kept under a Levite's care with the names still attached to them — Samuel's, Abner's, Joab's, and Saul's. All of it comes up the hill and goes into the treasuries of a building David never saw.

Then the assembly is called, and the date is given in a way that repays attention: all the men of Israel assembled before the king at the feast that is in the seventh month.
