The feast of the seventh month is Tabernacles, and Tabernacles is the week in which every Israelite leaves his house and lives in a shelter of branches, because the law says: so that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of Egypt.

So on the one week of the year when the whole nation is camping out in the open to remember that it once had no home, God is moved out of a tent into a house of stone and cedar. Israel goes into booths and the ark comes indoors, in the same week, by design.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the elders of Israel came, and the Levites took up the ark. And they brought up the ark, the tent of meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the tent; the Levitical priests brought them up. And King Solomon and all the congregation of Israel, who had assembled before him, were before the ark, sacrificing so many sheep and oxen that they could not be counted or numbered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all the elders of Israel came, and the Levites took up the ark.

Four words settle a question that had cost a life. The Levites took it up — on their shoulders, with the poles, as Moses commanded according to the word of the LORD. The last time an ark travelled in Israel it went on a new cart because nobody had checked, and a man put out his hand at a threshing floor and died there, and the king was angry and then frightened and then went and read the law. Nothing in this verse draws attention to any of that. It simply says who carried it.

Then verse 5, and in one clause it closes something that has been open since the ark first came to Jerusalem.

And they brought up the ark, the tent of meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the tent; the Levitical priests brought them up.

The tent of meeting. The tabernacle Moses made at Sinai, which had been standing on the high place at Gibeon with the bronze altar in front of it for two generations while the ark sat in a different tent six miles away on Zion. Israel's worship had been cut in half: song and the throne on one hill, sacrifice and the full order of the law on another, and neither site whole.

Now the old tent is folded up and carried into the new house, and the two halves are under one roof. David could not do it. He kept both, obediently, and handed the problem forward, and every arrangement he made in the last years of his life — the site bought at full price, the gold, the courses of priests and singers and doorkeepers — was aimed at this clause.

The sacrifices that day could not be counted. It is the same phrase used of the patriarchs' descendants and of the sand on the shore, and here it is used of animals dying in a courtyard because a nation had run out of ways to say thank you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — Two Tablets and Nothing Else
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests set the ark in the inner sanctuary underneath the wings of the cherubim, whose wings make a covering above the ark and its poles (vv. 7-8). The poles are left in, and are so long that their ends can be seen from the Holy Place though not from outside — and they are there to this day (v. 9). And the box is opened to the reader: there was nothing in the ark except the two tablets that Moses put there at Horeb (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Inside the most sacred object in Israel there is a copy of the law, and nothing else. Over it is a gold lid where blood was put once a year, and over that the wings. The commandments that condemn are in the box; the place where blood is applied is the roof of it.
verseByVerse.examples: The poles were never taken out, by explicit command. The ark is at rest in a permanent house and still carrying-ready, as though God would not have his people forget that he had spent four hundred years on the move with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place, in the inner sanctuary of the house, in the Most Holy Place, underneath the wings of the cherubim. The cherubim spread out their wings over the place of the ark, so that the cherubim made a covering above the ark and its poles. And the poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the Holy Place before the inner sanctuary, but they could not be seen from outside. And they are there to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ark goes into the innermost room, under the wings of the two great figures carved for it, and the wings made a covering above the ark and its poles. It is the tabernacle arrangement enlarged: gold over acacia wood, a lid, two cherubim, and God's promise to meet his people there.

Then a detail about the poles, and it takes a whole verse.

And the poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the Holy Place before the inner sanctuary, but they could not be seen from outside.

They were left in. That was commanded at Sinai — the poles shall remain in the rings of the ark, they shall not be taken from it — and it is a strange command for an object that was about to stop travelling. The ark is finally at rest, in a permanent house, on the hill God chose, and it is still rigged to be carried.

A priest standing in the Holy Place could see the two ends of the poles pushing against the veil from the other side. He could not see the ark. He could see that it was ready to move.

Then four words that have a shadow on them: And they are there to this day.

Whoever first wrote that sentence was writing while the poles were still there. The man who copied it into this book was not. By his time the house had been burned, the pillars broken up for their bronze, the vessels carried to Babylon, and the ark itself gone without a word of explanation from anybody. He left the sentence standing. His readers, walking past a smaller temple with an empty room at the heart of it, read to this day and knew exactly what day it had been.

verseByVerse.quote: There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets that Moses put there at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel, when they came out of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets that Moses put there at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel, when they came out of Egypt.

Nothing else. The jar of manna and the rod that budded had been set down before the testimony rather than in it, and by Solomon's day they are not mentioned. What is inside the most sacred object in the nation is two slabs of stone with ten commandments cut into them.

Consider what that means as an arrangement of furniture. At the centre of the house, in the room nobody enters, inside a box nobody touches, is the law — the covenant Israel had already broken before Moses got down the mountain with it, and had gone on breaking ever since. It is the evidence against them, and it is kept in the holiest place they have.

And on top of the box is a lid of solid gold, and once a year the high priest goes in with blood and puts it on that lid, between the wings, directly above the tablets. The law is not removed and it is not amended. It is covered, and the covering is blood.

The letter to the Romans takes the name of that lid and gives it to a person: God put Christ forward as the mercy seat, in his blood, to be received by faith. What was hidden in the dark of an inner room, above a broken covenant, with one man allowed near it one day a year, has been set out in the open street where anyone may look. The tablets are still in the box. The blood is still on the lid. The room is no longer shut.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every priest present has consecrated himself without regard to their divisions (v. 11); the singers — Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun with their sons and kinsmen, in fine linen — stand east of the altar with a hundred and twenty trumpeters (v. 12); and their duty is to make themselves heard in unison in praise and thanksgiving to the LORD. When the song goes up — For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever — the house, the house of the LORD, was filled with a cloud (v. 13), so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of God (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The rota is suspended. Twenty-four courses were drawn by lot so that every family would have its week, and on this day the roster is set aside and every priest in Israel is on duty at once.
verseByVerse.examples: The same thing happened to Moses. When the tabernacle was finished the cloud settled on it and the glory filled it and he could not go in. The men who built the house were the first people it shut out.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the priests came out of the Holy Place (for all the priests who were present had consecrated themselves, without regard to their divisions, and all the Levitical singers, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, their sons and kinsmen, arrayed in fine linen, with cymbals, harps, and lyres, stood east of the altar with 120 priests who were trumpeters; and it was the duty of the trumpeters and singers to make themselves heard in unison in praise and thanksgiving to the LORD), and when the song was raised, with trumpets and cymbals and other musical instruments, in praise to the LORD, "For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever," the house, the house of the LORD, was filled with a cloud,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the music, and the Chronicler slows down to say who was there.

First the priests, and a clause easy to run past: for all the priests who were present had consecrated themselves, without regard to their divisions.

The divisions are the twenty-four courses drawn by lot in front of David and Zadok and a Levite scribe, so that every family in the priesthood would get its week and nobody could arrange to be on duty at the great feasts. On this day the roster is set aside. Every priest in Israel has purified himself and every one of them is serving at once, and the fairest rota ever devised is suspended because there is a day it cannot cope with.

Then the singers, and the three names are the three from the ark's first journey: Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, with their sons and kinsmen, dressed in fine linen, standing east of the altar with a hundred and twenty priests blowing trumpets.

And their duty is described in a phrase worth holding: to make themselves heard in unison in praise and thanksgiving to the LORD. The Hebrew is plainer — to be as one. Not merely together in time, but one voice, so that a listener in the court could not tell the singers apart.

What they sang is quoted, and it is six words: For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever.

Those are the words David appointed on the afternoon the ark came into Jerusalem and stood in a tent. It has been sung every day since by men whose whole job was thanksgiving, on a rota, in all weathers. Now the house is finished and the ark is in it and the nation is assembled, and what they reach for is the sentence they already knew.

verseByVerse.quote: so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house, the house of the LORD, was filled with a cloud, so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of God.

The text stutters. The house, the house of the LORD — as though the writer, having got there, cannot get the words out in one go.

This has happened once before. When the tabernacle was finished in the wilderness and everything had been done as the LORD commanded Moses, the cloud covered the tent and the glory of the LORD filled it, and Moses was not able to enter. The man who built it was the first person it shut out, and now the same thing happens to a courtyard full of consecrated priests in fine linen who have spent seven years getting ready.

They could not stand. There is no rebuke in it, no fire, nobody struck down. The room simply became unusable for the purpose it had been built for, because the one it was built for had arrived.

Notice the order the Chronicler gives. He does not write that the priests prayed the cloud down, and the song is not a technique — what they sang was a sentence about God's character, not about their own longing, and the glory came while it was being sung by men who had put the rota aside so that everyone could be in the room. It would be a mistake to read this as a method. It is a record of what happened when a nation finally did what it had been told, in the way it had been told, with one voice.

And a thousand years later the glory came again, and there was no cloud and nobody was shut out. He was wrapped in cloth and put in a feeding trough, and the word John used for it was the word for pitching a tent: he tabernacled among us, and we have seen his glory. Solomon's priests backed out of a room they could not stand in. The ones who came to that glory were sat down and fed.

6.title: Toward This Place
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Solomon said, "The LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness.<sup>2</sup>But I have built you an exalted house, a place for you to dwell in forever."<sup>3</sup>Then the king turned around and blessed all the assembly of Israel, while all the assembly of Israel stood.<sup>4</sup>And he said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who with his hand has fulfilled what he promised with his mouth to David my father, saying,<sup>5</sup>'Since the day that I brought my people out of the land of Egypt, I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house, that my name might be there, and I chose no man as prince over my people Israel;<sup>6</sup>but I have chosen Jerusalem that my name may be there, and I have chosen David to be over my people Israel.'<sup>7</sup>Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>8</sup>But the LORD said to David my father, 'Whereas it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart.<sup>9</sup>Nevertheless, it is not you who shall build the house, but your son who shall be born to you shall build the house for my name.'<sup>10</sup>Now the LORD has fulfilled his promise that he made. For I have risen in the place of David my father and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised, and I have built the house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>11</sup>And there I have set the ark, in which is the covenant of the LORD that he made with the people of Israel."<sup>12</sup>Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in the presence of all the assembly of Israel and spread out his hands.<sup>13</sup>Solomon had made a bronze platform five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high, and had set it in the court, and he stood on it. Then he knelt on his knees in the presence of all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven,<sup>14</sup>and said, "O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like you, in heaven or on earth, keeping covenant and showing steadfast love to your servants who walk before you with all their heart,<sup>15</sup>who have kept with your servant David my father what you declared to him. You spoke with your mouth, and with your hand have fulfilled it this day.<sup>16</sup>Now therefore, O LORD, God of Israel, keep for your servant David my father what you have promised him, saying, 'You shall not lack a man to sit before me on the throne of Israel, if only your sons pay close attention to their way, to walk in my law as you have walked before me.'<sup>17</sup>Now therefore, O LORD, God of Israel, let your word be confirmed, which you have spoken to your servant David.<sup>18</sup>"But will God indeed dwell with man on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you, how much less this house that I have built!<sup>19</sup>Yet have regard to the prayer of your servant and to his plea, O LORD my God, listening to the cry and to the prayer that your servant prays before you,<sup>20</sup>that your eyes may be open day and night toward this house, the place where you have promised to set your name, that you may listen to the prayer that your servant offers toward this place.<sup>21</sup>And listen to the pleas of your servant and of your people Israel, when they pray toward this place. And listen from heaven your dwelling place, and when you hear, forgive.<sup>22</sup>"If a man sins against his neighbor and is made to take an oath and comes and swears his oath before your altar in this house,<sup>23</sup>then hear from heaven and act and judge your servants, repaying the guilty by bringing his conduct on his own head, and vindicating the righteous by rewarding him according to his righteousness.<sup>24</sup>"If your people Israel are defeated before the enemy because they have sinned against you, and they turn again and acknowledge your name and pray and plead with you in this house,<sup>25</sup>then hear from heaven and forgive the sin of your people Israel and bring them again to the land that you gave to them and to their fathers.<sup>26</sup>"When heaven is shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against you, if they pray toward this place and acknowledge your name and turn from their sin, when you afflict them,<sup>27</sup>then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel, when you teach them the good way in which they should walk, and grant rain upon your land, which you have given to your people as an inheritance.<sup>28</sup>"If there is famine in the land, if there is pestilence or blight or mildew or locust or caterpillar, if their enemies besiege them in the land at their gates, whatever 6.overview:
Solomon reads the cloud as the sign that God has moved in (vv. 1-2), turns from the house to bless the people, and rehearses God's own word — the choosing of a city and a man, and his father's refused ambition with the commendation attached to it (vv. 3-11). He mounts a bronze platform, kneels in front of the whole assembly, and prays (vv. 12-13): God is incomparable and keeps covenant (vv. 14-17); no house can contain him, so let his eyes be open toward this one (vv. 18-21). Seven petitions follow — an oath between neighbours, defeat, drought, plague, the foreigner, armies, and exile (vv. 22-39). It closes by quoting Psalm 132 and asking God to remember his steadfast love for David (vv. 40-42).

Chronicles alone records the platform and the kneeling, and Chronicles alone ends the prayer on the psalm about David's oath rather than on Moses and the Exodus.
6.theology:
The prayer never once confuses the two addresses. Listen from heaven your dwelling place is said four times; the house is only ever what a person prays toward. That distinction is why the prayer outlived the building: a man in Babylon could still face that direction and be heard, because the hearing had never been done from inside it. And verse 18 asks the question the rest of Scripture answers — will God indeed dwell with man on the earth? — to which John's answer is that the Word pitched his tent among us, and Revelation's is that the dwelling place of God is with man.

Verse 8 holds two things most people cannot hold at once: God refuses David and says you did well that it was in your heart. The no was about which man would build. It was not a verdict on the wanting — and a man who grasps that can spend forty years serving an ambition he has been told he will never see.
6.examples:
He knelt. On a platform three cubits high, built so the nation could see him, on the day his greatest work was finished — and the other account of that day lets it slip only in a passing clause about him getting up again.

The first of the seven petitions is a quarrel between neighbours. Before the famines and the armies and the exile, the most expensive building in Israel is put at the disposal of one man who has been wronged by somebody down the road.

For his own people Solomon asks forgiveness. For the foreigner he asks God to do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you — everything, unqualified — so that the news would travel to countries the temple would never reach.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — He Spoke With His Mouth and Fulfilled With His Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With the cloud still in the room Solomon reads it: the LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness. But I have built you an exalted house (vv. 1-2). He turns from the house to the people and blesses them (v. 3), and the blessing is a review of God's own word — who with his hand has fulfilled what he promised with his mouth (v. 4) — with the double choosing quoted: no city and no man, then Jerusalem and David (vv. 5-6). Then his father's refused ambition, and the sentence God attached to it: you did well that it was in your heart (vv. 7-9). And the summary: the promise is kept, the son reigns, the house is built, and there I have set the ark (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: God said no to David and commended him in the same breath. The refusal was about which man would build; it was not a verdict on the wanting, and the son repeats the commendation aloud in front of the nation on the day the thing is finished.
verseByVerse.examples: Twice in this section God's mouth and God's hand are named together. What he says with the one he does with the other, and the building everybody is standing in is the evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon said, "The LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness. But I have built you an exalted house, a place for you to dwell in forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cloud is still in the building. The priests have backed out of a room they could not stand up in, the singers have stopped, and into that silence the king says the first thing anybody has said.

The LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness.

He is interpreting what has just happened, and he does it out of the law. At Sinai the people stood far off while Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was. The mountain burned with fire to the heart of heaven, with darkness, cloud and gloom. A psalm says he made darkness his covering, his canopy around him; another says clouds and thick darkness are all around him.

So the cloud is not an accident of weather and it is not a disaster. It is the signature. The God of Israel has always come in a darkness thick enough to hide him, and the reason is mercy rather than concealment: what is not veiled cannot be approached and lived through. Solomon looks at a room nobody can enter and concludes that God has moved in.

Then the sentence beside it. But I have built you an exalted house, a place for you to dwell in forever.

Thick darkness, and an exalted house. A God who hides himself, and a building of gold and cedar with his address on it. Solomon puts the two together without resolving them, which is the only honest thing to do with them, and the rest of his prayer will keep both hands on the problem.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king turned around and blessed all the assembly of Israel, while all the assembly of Israel stood. And he said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who with his hand has fulfilled what he promised with his mouth to David my father, saying, 'Since the day that I brought my people out of the land of Egypt, I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house, that my name might be there, and I chose no man as prince over my people Israel; but I have chosen Jerusalem that my name may be there, and I have chosen David to be over my people Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king turned around and blessed all the assembly of Israel, while all the assembly of Israel stood.

He had been facing the house. He turns his back on it to face the people, and the first thing he does on the greatest day of his reign is bless the congregation — which is what his father did when the ark came home, and what Aaron's sons were commissioned to do. The whole nation is standing.

And the blessing is not a wish. It is a recital of what God has said and done, and the two are welded: Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who with his hand has fulfilled what he promised with his mouth to David my father.

Mouth and hand. He will say it again in a few verses, and it is the plainest definition of faithfulness anyone has given: what God says with the one, he does with the other. The building they are standing in is the evidence, and Solomon offers it as evidence rather than as an achievement.

Then he quotes God directly, and the quotation is built as a pair of denials answered by a pair of choices. I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house, that my name might be there, and I chose no man as prince over my people Israel; but I have chosen Jerusalem that my name may be there, and I have chosen David to be over my people Israel.

For four hundred years, from the Exodus to the reign of Saul, God had picked no capital and no dynasty. The ark moved between Gilgal and Shiloh and Nob and Kiriath-jearim; the leadership passed from judge to judge with gaps in between. Then two choices, made together: a place and a person. A city for the name and a man for the throne. The temple and the covenant with David are not two subjects. They were chosen in the same sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. But the LORD said to David my father, 'Whereas it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart. Nevertheless, it is not you who shall build the house, but your son who shall be born to you shall build the house for my name.' Now the LORD has fulfilled his promise that he made. For I have risen in the place of David my father and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised, and I have built the house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. And there I have set the ark, in which is the covenant of the LORD that he made with the people of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Solomon tells the assembly about his father's disappointment, and he tells it straight.

Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. But the LORD said to David my father ...

Then comes the clause that is the reason this passage repays a long look.

Whereas it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart.

God refused him and commended him in one breath. Not: your motives were mixed. Not: you should have consulted me first. You did well that it was in your heart — the wanting itself is approved, on the record, by the one who said no to it.

Those two things are much harder to hold together than either on its own, and most people manage only one. A refusal usually feels like a judgement on the desire behind it, so a man who is turned down concludes either that he was wrong to want it or that God was unkind to withhold it. Here is a third possibility, stated by God himself: the desire was good, the answer is no, and both are final.

And look at how the son is described in verse 9: your son who shall be born to you shall build the house for my name. Not yet born. When God refused David, the man who would do the work did not exist, and the promise was made about somebody nobody in the room could have pointed to. David spent the rest of his life buying materials for a person he had not met.

What David did with that is the whole back end of the previous book. He bought the site, stockpiled the gold and the iron and the nails, drew up the plans, organised the priests and the singers and the doorkeepers, charged his son in public and prayed for his heart — for a building he had been told he would never enter. A man who believes his refused ambition was still good can spend forty years serving it.

Then the summing up: Now the LORD has fulfilled his promise that he made — I reign, the house stands, and there I have set the ark, in which is the covenant of the LORD that he made with the people of Israel. Everything in the sentence is God's doing except the setting down of the box, and even that is only putting a covenant where God said to put it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon has made a bronze platform, five cubits by five and three high, and set it in the court; he stands on it, and then he knelt on his knees in the presence of all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven (vv. 12-13). The prayer opens with God's incomparability and covenant faithfulness (vv. 14-15), asks him to keep the promise to David — quoting its condition, if only your sons pay close attention to their way (vv. 16-17) — and then stops to say what a temple cannot be: heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you, how much less this house that I have built! (v. 18). What he asks is that God's eyes be open toward the place and that he listen from heaven your dwelling place, and when you hear, forgive (vv. 19-21).
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer never confuses the two addresses. God's dwelling place is heaven; the house is what a person prays toward. Solomon has built the most expensive building in the nation's history and spends the dedication saying what it is not.
verseByVerse.examples: He knelt. A king on a platform in front of his whole kingdom went down on his knees, and the account in Kings only lets it slip at the end, when it mentions that he got up.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in the presence of all the assembly of Israel and spread out his hands. Solomon had made a bronze platform five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high, and had set it in the court, and he stood on it. Then he knelt on his knees in the presence of all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the posture, and Chronicles alone records it.

Solomon had made a bronze platform five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high, and had set it in the court, and he stood on it.

The account in Kings has no platform. And set the measurements beside another set: the bronze altar Bezalel made in the wilderness, which Solomon had been sacrificing on at Gibeon two chapters ago, was five cubits long, five cubits broad and three cubits high. The same three figures. Whether that was deliberate cannot be known, and the text does not say — but the king is standing in the temple court on a bronze structure the exact size of an altar, about to offer the only thing he has left to offer.

Then: he knelt on his knees in the presence of all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven.

He is on a platform three cubits high, built so that a nation could see him. And what they see is the king going down.

The other account of this day has him standing before the altar to pray, and only lets the truth out at the end, in a passing clause, when Solomon arose from before the altar of the LORD, from kneeling on his knees. Chronicles puts it where it belongs, in the middle of the sentence, in front of everybody. Israel watched its wealthiest and wisest king kneel down in public on the day his greatest work was finished, and the writer thought that was the detail to keep.

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like you, in heaven or on earth, keeping covenant and showing steadfast love to your servants who walk before you with all their heart, who have kept with your servant David my father what you declared to him. You spoke with your mouth, and with your hand have fulfilled it this day. Now therefore, O LORD, God of Israel, keep for your servant David my father what you have promised him, saying, 'You shall not lack a man to sit before me on the throne of Israel, if only your sons pay close attention to their way, to walk in my law as you have walked before me.' Now therefore, O LORD, God of Israel, let your word be confirmed, which you have spoken to your servant David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer opens with a comparison and finds nothing to compare. O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like you, in heaven or on earth. Not the best of them; there is no other in either place.

Then what he is like: keeping covenant and showing steadfast love to your servants who walk before you with all their heart. Covenant and steadfast love, held together — the legal word and the warm one. God is bound, and he is willing.

And the evidence is in the room: You spoke with your mouth, and with your hand have fulfilled it this day. Second time in eleven verses. Solomon keeps returning to it because it is the only argument he has, and because it is enough.

Then he asks God to keep the rest of what he said — and quotes the promise with its condition attached. You shall not lack a man to sit before me on the throne of Israel, if only your sons pay close attention to their way, to walk in my law as you have walked before me.

Then verse 17, and it is the shortest request in the prayer: let your word be confirmed, which you have spoken to your servant David. He is not asking God to add anything. He is asking him to stand by a sentence already spoken — which is what his father asked for on the night it was spoken, and what Solomon asked for at Gibeon.

That if only is interesting, because this book has been leaving it out. When Nathan brought the covenant, Chronicles printed the promise without the discipline clause. When God appeared at Gibeon and granted wisdom, Chronicles printed the gift and dropped the condition the other account attaches. Here, at last, the condition is stated — and it is stated by the king himself, in prayer, about his own sons. The Chronicler will not use it as a threat. He lets Solomon say it as a request.

verseByVerse.quote: "But will God indeed dwell with man on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you, how much less this house that I have built! Yet have regard to the prayer of your servant and to his plea, O LORD my God, listening to the cry and to the prayer that your servant prays before you, that your eyes may be open day and night toward this house, the place where you have promised to set your name, that you may listen to the prayer that your servant offers toward this place. And listen to the pleas of your servant and of your people Israel, when they pray toward this place. And listen from heaven your dwelling place, and when you hear, forgive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then, in the middle of the dedication of the building he has spent seven years raising, Solomon says this.

But will God indeed dwell with man on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you, how much less this house that I have built!

He said it in the letter that ordered the timber, before a stone was cut. He says it again with the gold on the walls and the cloud in the room and a hundred thousand people watching. The house is a marvel and the house is not the point, and the man who built it is the one insisting on it.

The question at the front of that verse is the one the whole Bible is answering. Will God dwell with man on the earth? Solomon asks it as a genuine question and does not answer it. Centuries later a man who had put his hands on the answer wrote that the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us, and we have seen his glory. And near the end of Revelation a loud voice from the throne says that the dwelling place of God is with man.

What Solomon asks for instead is attention. That your eyes may be open day and night toward this house, the place where you have promised to set your name. Not that God would live in it — that he would look at it.

And the geography stays exact all the way through. Listen from heaven your dwelling place. God's address is heaven. The house is what a person turns toward. Nothing in the prayer confuses the two, which is why the prayer survived the building's destruction — a man in Babylon could still face that direction and be heard, because the hearing had never been done from there in the first place.

Verse 19 piles up the words for asking until they run over each other — the prayer of your servant and ... his plea ... the cry and ... the prayer that your servant prays before you. Four nouns for the same act in one sentence. He is not being decorative. A man who is about to describe famine and siege and captivity is reaching for every word his language has for a person trying to get God's attention.

Then three words that will come back: and when you hear, forgive. Not when you hear, act, or answer, or intervene. Forgive, and it is asked five times before the prayer is done. Solomon has worked out what his nation will mostly need.

Count the refrain itself while it goes past, because it is the spine of everything from here to verse 39. Hear from heaven — eight times, once in every petition and once here at the start. Four of the eight add the same three words: your dwelling place. Eight times over, in a building that had just cost seven years and more gold than anyone could weigh, the king points away from it and upward.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The requests begin, and each is a case. A man swearing an oath at the altar over a wrong done to his neighbour (vv. 22-23). The nation defeated because it has sinned, turning back and praying (vv. 24-25). The sky shut and no rain, until they turn — when you teach them the good way in which they should walk (vv. 26-27). Then a catalogue that leaves nothing out: famine, pestilence, blight, mildew, locust, caterpillar, siege, whatever plague, whatever sickness there is — and inside the catalogue one man, each knowing his own affliction and his own sorrow, stretching out his hands (vv. 28-29). The ground of the asking is that God alone reads hearts (vv. 30-31).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 30 makes the one claim about God that the whole prayer rests on: you, you only, know the hearts of the children of mankind. It is his father's sentence to him at the handover — the LORD searches all hearts — turned round and prayed back.
verseByVerse.examples: In the middle of a national disaster list stands a single person with his own particular grief, named as such. Solomon asks God to render to each, and the plague and the locust do not blur the individual out.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man sins against his neighbor and is made to take an oath and comes and swears his oath before your altar in this house, then hear from heaven and act and judge your servants, repaying the guilty by bringing his conduct on his own head, and vindicating the righteous by rewarding him according to his righteousness. "If your people Israel are defeated before the enemy because they have sinned against you, and they turn again and acknowledge your name and pray and plead with you in this house, then hear from heaven and forgive the sin of your people Israel and bring them again to the land that you gave to them and to their fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the requests, and they are cases rather than themes — seven of them, each beginning with an if or a when.

The first is the smallest and it is domestic. If a man sins against his neighbor and is made to take an oath and comes and swears his oath before your altar in this house. Two men in a village, a dispute nobody can settle, and a procedure: the accused swears at the altar, and God is asked to sort out who is lying — repaying the guilty by bringing his conduct on his own head, and vindicating the righteous.

The most magnificent building in Israel is put at the disposal of a quarrel between neighbours, and the case is listed first. Before the armies and the famines and the exile, a man who has been wronged by somebody down the road.

The second is national and the diagnosis is blunt. If your people Israel are defeated before the enemy because they have sinned against you. Not if they are defeated — when they are, the cause is named in advance and it is not the enemy's strength.

What they do about it has three verbs: they turn again and acknowledge your name and pray. Turning first. Then owning the name they had abandoned. Then asking. What Solomon requests is that God bring them again to the land — the first hint in the prayer that being out of it is a possibility.

verseByVerse.quote: "When heaven is shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against you, if they pray toward this place and acknowledge your name and turn from their sin, when you afflict them, then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel, when you teach them the good way in which they should walk, and grant rain upon your land, which you have given to your people as an inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third case is drought. When heaven is shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against you.

Notice the word this time. The first two cases were introduced with if. This one is when. In a country farming rain-fed hills with no great river, drought is not a hypothesis; it is a matter of time, and Solomon prays for it as a certainty.

The remedy is the same shape: pray toward the place, acknowledge the name, turn from the sin — and then a clause that is easy to miss and worth stopping on. They turn from their sin when you afflict them.

The affliction is God's, and it is aimed at producing the turning. The shut sky is not him losing interest. It is him getting their attention in the one currency an agricultural nation cannot ignore.

The request that follows has two halves most people would not put together. Then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your servants ... when you teach them the good way in which they should walk, and grant rain upon your land. Forgive, teach, and send rain. He does not ask for the weather to change and leave it there. He asks for instruction in the middle of the drought, as though the point of the whole episode were that they should learn to walk somewhere better.

verseByVerse.quote: "If there is famine in the land, if there is pestilence or blight or mildew or locust or caterpillar, if their enemies besiege them in the land at their gates, whatever plague, whatever sickness there is, whatever prayer, whatever plea is made by any man or by all your people Israel, each knowing his own affliction and his own sorrow and stretching out his hands toward this house, then hear from heaven your dwelling place and forgive and render to each whose heart you know, according to all his ways, for you, you only, know the hearts of the children of mankind, that they may fear you and walk in your ways all the days that they live in the land that you gave to our fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth case is a catalogue, and it is written to leave nothing out. If there is famine in the land, if there is pestilence or blight or mildew or locust or caterpillar, if their enemies besiege them in the land at their gates, whatever plague, whatever sickness there is.

Eight named disasters and then two open categories to catch anything he has forgotten. Solomon is trying to build a prayer with no gaps in it, because he is praying for four hundred years of a nation he will not live to see.

Halfway through the catalogue the camera moves in.

Whatever prayer, whatever plea is made by any man or by all your people Israel, each knowing his own affliction and his own sorrow and stretching out his hands toward this house.

Any man, or all of them. And that phrase — each knowing his own affliction and his own sorrow — is one that only somebody who has watched people suffer would write. A national calamity is a single word in a chronicle and a thousand separate rooms at the time. The locust took everybody's crop and each family sat with its own particular version of it. Solomon prays for the aggregate and then insists on the individual inside it.

And the ground he gives is the ground his father gave him. Render to each whose heart you know, according to all his ways, for you, you only, know the hearts of the children of mankind.

And verse 31 gives the point of the whole exercise, which is not relief. That they may fear you and walk in your ways all the days that they live in the land that you gave to our fathers.

The rain, the healing, the lifted siege — none of them is the object. Solomon asks for the disaster to be answered so that the people will fear God and walk in his ways for the rest of their lives, which means he is treating every calamity in the list as an opportunity rather than an interruption. He is not asking for a comfortable nation. He is asking for one that has learned something and kept it.

David had said it to him at the handover, in front of the whole assembly: the LORD searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought. The son took it in, and here he turns it into the reason God can be trusted with a nation's grief. Nobody else can tell the difference between the man who is sorry and the man who is only frightened. God can, and that is why Solomon is willing to ask him to render to each.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–39 — The Foreigner, and the Exile
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fifth petition is the foreigner: someone who is not of your people Israel, come from a far country because he has heard of the great name and the outstretched arm — and for him Solomon asks God to do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you, so that all the peoples of the earth may know the name (vv. 32-33). Then armies sent out (vv. 34-35). And last, the one that would matter most: if they sin against you — for there is no one who does not sin — and are carried captive far off, and turn their heart in that land and pray toward the city, then hear from heaven your dwelling place ... and forgive your people (vv. 36-39).
verseByVerse.theology: For Israel Solomon asks forgiveness. For the foreigner he asks God to do everything the man requests, and gives the reason: so that the whole earth may learn the name. The widest petition in the prayer is the one made on behalf of an outsider.
verseByVerse.examples: The last case is exile, prayed four hundred years before it happened. The people who first read this book were living inside verse 38 — praying toward a city they had been carried away from — and Daniel opened his windows toward Jerusalem three times a day because of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Likewise, when a foreigner, who is not of your people Israel, comes from a far country for the sake of your great name and your mighty hand and your outstretched arm, when he comes and prays toward this house, hear from heaven your dwelling place and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you, in order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name and fear you, as do your people Israel, and that they may know that this house that I have built is called by your name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fifth petition is the one nobody would have predicted, and it sits at the centre of the seven.

Likewise, when a foreigner, who is not of your people Israel, comes from a far country for the sake of your great name and your mighty hand and your outstretched arm, when he comes and prays toward this house.

Not a resident alien quarrying stone in the hills. Somebody from a far country who has heard something and travelled. And the thing he has heard is not that Israel is prosperous or that its temple is a spectacle; it is your great name and your mighty hand and your outstretched arm — the language of the Exodus, which is to say the story of what this God did for slaves.

Then the asking, and it is not what Solomon asks for his own people. For Israel he has been requesting forgiveness and restoration. For the foreigner: do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you.

All of it. No qualification, no condition, no probation. The king of Israel stands in the court of the temple on the day of its dedication and asks God to give a Gentile whatever he asks for.

And the reason is given, and it is not politeness. In order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name and fear you, as do your people Israel, and that they may know that this house that I have built is called by your name. The point of answering the outsider is that the news should travel. A foreigner who goes home with his prayer answered is a witness in a country the temple will never reach.

Isaiah heard God say the same thing centuries later, and more sharply — that the foreigners who joined themselves to the LORD would be brought to his holy mountain and made joyful in his house of prayer, for his house would be called a house of prayer for all peoples. And on a Monday in the last week of his life, the Son of David walked into that court, saw it filled with tables, and drove them out quoting that verse — because the traders had set up in the one part of the building where the foreigner of verse 32 was allowed to stand.

verseByVerse.quote: "If your people go out to battle against their enemies, by whatever way you shall send them, and they pray to you toward this city that you have chosen and the house that I have built for your name, then hear from heaven their prayer and their plea, and maintain their cause.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sixth case is short and it is the only one where Israel has done nothing wrong. If your people go out to battle against their enemies, by whatever way you shall send them.

The clause in the middle is the whole condition: by whatever way you shall send them. Not every war qualifies. The prayer covers armies God has dispatched, and says nothing at all about the others.

And what they do at the far end of the campaign is pray toward the city and the house — which is a strange military instruction and a very old one. Soldiers a hundred miles from Jerusalem, in a field, turning to face a building. Solomon asks God to maintain their cause, which is a courtroom phrase rather than a battlefield one. He wants the verdict to be right more than he wants the fight to be won.

verseByVerse.quote: "If they sin against you— for there is no one who does not sin—and you are angry with them and give them to an enemy, so that they are carried away captive to a land far or near, yet if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive, and repent and plead with you in the land of their captivity, saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly,' if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their captivity to which they were carried captive, and pray toward their land, which you gave to their fathers, the city that you have chosen and the house that I have built for your name, then hear from heaven your dwelling place their prayer and their pleas, and maintain their cause and forgive your people who have sinned against you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventh case is the longest, and it is the one the people who first read this book were living inside.

If they sin against you — for there is no one who does not sin — and you are angry with them and give them to an enemy, so that they are carried away captive to a land far or near.

The parenthesis stops the sentence dead. For there is no one who does not sin. It is not a rhetorical flourish; it is the reason the case has to be prayed for at all. Solomon is not entertaining an unlikely scenario. He is stating that the thing which will eventually destroy the nation is already present in every person in the courtyard, including the man on the platform, and that on a long enough timescale it is certain.

So he prays for the exile on the day the temple opens. The building is four hours old and its dedication includes a petition for the generation that will watch it burn.

What he asks them to do is described with unusual care: if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive, and repent and plead with you — and he even supplies the words, we have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly — if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their captivity ... and pray toward their land ... the city that you have chosen and the house that I have built for your name.

Four centuries later a civil servant in Babylon went up to his roof chamber, where the windows were open toward Jerusalem, and got down on his knees three times a day and prayed, and went on doing it after it had been made a capital offence. He was doing what this verse told him to do, in a city the length of a desert away, facing a hill with a ruin on it.

The petition itself is the same for the seventh time: hear from heaven your dwelling place ... and forgive your people who have sinned against you. The house may be gone. The direction still works, because God was never listening from inside it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–42 — Arise, O LORD, to Your Resting Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prayer ends by asking God to settle. Now, O my God, let your eyes be open and your ears attentive to the prayer of this place (v. 40). Then words that are not Solomon's own: arise, O LORD God, and go to your resting place, you and the ark of your might. Let your priests, O LORD God, be clothed with salvation, and let your saints rejoice in your goodness (v. 41). And the last line: O LORD God, do not turn away the face of your anointed one! Remember your steadfast love for David your servant (v. 42).
verseByVerse.theology: The account in Kings closes this prayer on the Exodus and on Moses. Chronicles closes it by quoting the psalm about David swearing he would not go up to his bed until he found a place for the LORD. The son finishes his father's psalm on the day his father's project is opened.
verseByVerse.examples: Its final phrase is the steadfast love promised to David. Isaiah would offer that same phrase to anybody who was thirsty, as an everlasting covenant, and the apostles preached that it was handed over on the morning the tomb was found empty.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, O my God, let your eyes be open and your ears attentive to the prayer of this place. "And now arise, O LORD God, and go to your resting place, you and the ark of your might. Let your priests, O LORD God, be clothed with salvation, and let your saints rejoice in your goodness. O LORD God, do not turn away the face of your anointed one! Remember your steadfast love for David your servant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now, O my God, let your eyes be open and your ears attentive to the prayer of this place. Eyes and ears — the two things he has been asking for since verse 20, gathered into one line.

And then the prayer ends with words that are not Solomon's own, and this is where Chronicles parts company with the other account entirely. In Kings the dedication closes on the Exodus, on Israel as God's inheritance, on Moses. Here it closes with a psalm.

And now arise, O LORD God, and go to your resting place, you and the ark of your might. Let your priests, O LORD God, be clothed with salvation, and let your saints rejoice in your goodness.

That is Psalm 132, and Psalm 132 is about his father. It is the psalm of the oath David swore — that he would not come into his house or go up to his bed or give sleep to his eyes until he found a place for the LORD, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob. The son ends the dedication by quoting the song about the vow, on the day the vow is discharged.

And the word he asks God to accept is resting place. It is the word David used when he stood up in front of the assembly and said he had it in his heart to build a house of rest for the ark of the covenant and for the footstool of our God. Everything since has been about getting a God who moved from tent to tent for four hundred years to sit down.

Then the last line of the longest prayer in the Old Testament. O LORD God, do not turn away the face of your anointed one! Remember your steadfast love for David your servant.

He does not end on the building. He ends on a promise made to his father, and asks God to remember it — which is what the whole family seems to have prayed. And the phrase he finishes with went on ahead of him. Isaiah stood in front of people who had nothing and told them to come and buy without money, and said God would make with them an everlasting covenant: my steadfast, sure love for David. Paul stood up in a synagogue in Antioch and said that God had given those holy and sure blessings of David by raising Jesus from the dead, never to see corruption again.

The house Solomon dedicated stood four hundred years and was burned. The steadfast love for David was handed over on the third day, and it does not need a room.

7.title: If My People
7.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as Solomon finished his prayer, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices, and the glory of the LORD filled the temple.<sup>2</sup>And the priests could not enter the house of the LORD, because the glory of the LORD filled the LORD's house.<sup>3</sup>When all the people of Israel saw the fire come down and the glory of the LORD on the temple, they bowed down with their faces to the ground on the pavement and worshiped and gave thanks to the LORD, saying, "For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever."<sup>4</sup>Then the king and all the people offered sacrifice before the LORD.<sup>5</sup>King Solomon offered as a sacrifice 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. So the king and all the people dedicated the house of God.<sup>6</sup>The priests stood at their posts; the Levites also, with the instruments for music to the LORD that King David had made for giving thanks to the LORD— for his steadfast love endures forever—whenever David offered praises by their ministry; opposite them the priests sounded trumpets, and all Israel stood.<sup>7</sup>And Solomon consecrated the middle of the court that was before the house of the LORD, for there he offered the burnt offering and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar Solomon had made could not hold the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat.<sup>8</sup>At that time Solomon held the feast for seven days, and all Israel with him, a very great assembly, from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt.<sup>9</sup>And on the eighth day they held a solemn assembly, for they had kept the dedication of the altar seven days and the feast seven days.<sup>10</sup>On the twenty-third day of the seventh month he sent the people away to their homes, joyful and glad of heart for the prosperity that the LORD had granted to David and to Solomon and to Israel his people.<sup>11</sup>Thus Solomon finished the house of the LORD and the king's house. All that Solomon had planned to do in the house of the LORD and in his own house he successfully accomplished.<sup>12</sup>Then the LORD appeared to Solomon in the night and said to him: "I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice.<sup>13</sup>When I shut up the heavens so that there is no rain, or command the locust to devour the land, or send pestilence among my people,<sup>14</sup>if my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land.<sup>15</sup>Now my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to the prayer that is made in this place.<sup>16</sup>For now I have chosen and consecrated this house that my name may be there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time.<sup>17</sup>And as for you, if you will walk before me as David your father walked, doing according to all that I have commanded you and keeping my statutes and my rules,<sup>18</sup>then I will establish your royal throne, as I covenanted with David your father, saying, 'You shall not lack a man to rule Israel.'<sup>19</sup>"But if you turn aside and forsake my statutes and my commandments that I have set before you, and go and serve other gods and worship them,<sup>20</sup>then I will pluck you up from my land that I have given you, and this house that I have consecrated for my name, I will cast out of my sight, and I will make it a proverb and a byword among all peoples.<sup>21</sup>And at this house, which was exalted, everyone passing by will be astonished and say, 'Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house?'<sup>22</sup>Then they will say, 'Because they abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers who brought them out of the land of Egypt, and laid hold on other gods and worshiped them and served them. Therefore he has brought all this disaster on them.'"
7.overview:
Fire falls the moment Solomon stops praying, the glory fills the house, and the priests are shut out again; the whole nation goes face-down on the pavement singing the choir's own line (vv. 1-3). Enormous offerings follow, played in on David's instruments, and the courtyard has to be consecrated because the altar cannot cope (vv. 4-7). Two weeks of feast end with the people sent home glad (vv. 8-11). Then God appears by night: he has heard, and names the building a house of sacrifice (v. 12); he takes responsibility for drought, locust and plague, and gives the promise the book turns on (vv. 13-14); he grants Solomon's request for eyes and ears and adds his heart (vv. 15-16). And he sets out the condition, the ruin, and the epitaph (vv. 17-22).

The fire is Chronicles' own — Kings has none here. It is the second time God has lit an altar on this hill.
7.theology:
Verse 14 is the sentence the whole book is built on, and verse 13 is the half that gets left off. Before the invitation there is a claim: I shut up the heavens ... I command the locust ... I send pestilence. The one who offers the remedy is the one who sent the trouble, and the three disasters he names are the ones Solomon had just prayed about. Four verbs are asked of the people — humble themselves, pray, seek my face, turn — and the fourth keeps the first three from becoming a technique. Three are promised: hear, forgive, heal, in that order, with the land last.

And my people who are called by my name means those over whom his name has been called: a covenant people, at a temple he had chosen, about a land he had given by oath. It is not a formula for any country wanting better harvests. What carries over is the people — those over whom his name is now called, who were bought at a price and are called by it.

Then the warning, spoken the same night: the house he has just consecrated can be cast out of his sight, and the reason is supplied in advance. The last chapter of this book reports it in almost the same words.
7.examples:
Solomon asked God for open eyes and attentive ears. God granted both in the same words and then said my eyes and my heart will be there for all time. Nobody asks a king for his heart. It was volunteered.

The largest altar ever built in Israel was too small on its first working day, and the king had to consecrate the paving around it. Everything about that house was built at the limit of what a nation could manage, and the first thing it did was overflow.

The people lying on the pavement already knew the words. The Levites had been singing that one line every morning and evening for forty years, and on the day it mattered the whole country could say it without being taught.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Fire, and an Altar Too Small
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As soon as Solomon finished his prayer, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices, and the glory of the LORD filled the temple (v. 1), and the priests are shut out a second time (v. 2). The people go face-down on the pavement and say the choir's own words — for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever (v. 3). Twenty-two thousand oxen and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep are offered (vv. 4-5); the Levites play the instruments that King David had made (v. 6); and the court itself has to be consecrated for sacrifice, because the bronze altar Solomon had made could not hold what was brought (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: God has lit an altar three times in this history: once at the tabernacle when Aaron had finished his first offering, once on this very threshing floor when a plague stopped, and now. Fire from heaven is how he signs for a place, and this is the second time he has signed for this one.
verseByVerse.examples: The altar was thirty feet square and it was not big enough. On its first working day the largest altar Israel ever built was overwhelmed, and the king had to consecrate the middle of the courtyard to take the overflow.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Solomon finished his prayer, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices, and the glory of the LORD filled the temple. And the priests could not enter the house of the LORD, because the glory of the LORD filled the LORD's house. When all the people of Israel saw the fire come down and the glory of the LORD on the temple, they bowed down with their faces to the ground on the pavement and worshiped and gave thanks to the LORD, saying, "For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As soon as Solomon finished his prayer, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices, and the glory of the LORD filled the temple.

Read the first three words again. Not that night, not the following week. The last word of the longest prayer in the Old Testament had barely left the man's mouth.

The other account of this day has no fire in it at all. Only this book records it, and only this book has recorded the other two occasions. When Aaron came down from making the first offering at the tabernacle and blessed the people, fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering, and the people shouted and fell on their faces. And on this hill, on a threshing floor bought at full price with seventy thousand people dead of a plague, David built an altar and called on the LORD, and the LORD answered him with fire from heaven.

So this is the second time God has set light to an altar on this exact patch of rock. The first time it was to stop a judgement and to mark the ground. Now the building has gone up over the place, and he does it again.

Then the priests, for the second time in three chapters, cannot get in. They could not stand to minister when the ark came in; now they cannot enter at all.

And the people do something the text is careful to record. When all the people of Israel saw the fire come down and the glory of the LORD on the temple, they bowed down with their faces to the ground on the pavement and worshiped and gave thanks to the LORD, saying, For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever.

That is the choir's line. Two chapters ago it belonged to Asaph and Heman and Jeduthun, trained singers in fine linen standing east of the altar. Here it is being said by farmers and soldiers lying face-down on paving stones. The professionals had been singing it every morning and evening for forty years, and on the one day it mattered most the whole nation already knew the words.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king and all the people offered sacrifice before the LORD. King Solomon offered as a sacrifice 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. So the king and all the people dedicated the house of God. The priests stood at their posts; the Levites also, with the instruments for music to the LORD that King David had made for giving thanks to the LORD— for his steadfast love endures forever—whenever David offered praises by their ministry; opposite them the priests sounded trumpets, and all Israel stood. And Solomon consecrated the middle of the court that was before the house of the LORD, for there he offered the burnt offering and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar Solomon had made could not hold the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The offerings are counted and the figures are hard to take in: twenty-two thousand oxen and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep. At that scale it is not an event but a fortnight of work, with the whole priesthood on duty and the courtyard running with blood from one end of the day to the other.

The Levites are at their posts with the instruments for music to the LORD that King David had made for giving thanks to the LORD — and the refrain is quoted again in the middle of the sentence, for his steadfast love endures forever, as though the writer cannot mention the instruments without the words that went with them. David had made those instruments with his own hands for a house he was told he would not build. They are being played in it.

Then a detail that is almost comic if you have read chapter 4. And Solomon consecrated the middle of the court that was before the house of the LORD ... because the bronze altar Solomon had made could not hold the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat.

That altar was thirty feet square and fifteen feet high, sixteen times the area of the one Bezalel made in the wilderness, and the largest ever built in Israel. On its first working day it was not big enough. They had to consecrate the paving around it and use the courtyard.

There is something in that worth keeping. Everything about this house was built at the limit of what a nation could manage, and the first thing it did was overflow. The vessel was always going to be too small for what it was made to hold.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–11 — Seven Days, and Seven More
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon keeps the feast for seven days with a very great assembly, from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt (v. 8), and on the eighth day they hold a solemn assembly, having kept the dedication seven days and the feast seven days (v. 9). On the twenty-third of the seventh month he sends them home joyful and glad of heart for the prosperity that the LORD had granted to David and to Solomon and to Israel his people (v. 10). And the building is signed off: Thus Solomon finished the house of the LORD and the king's house (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The gladness in verse 10 is credited to three parties in one line — David, Solomon, and Israel — and to the LORD who granted it. The dead king is named alongside the living one, at a dedication he did not live to attend.
verseByVerse.examples: Two weeks. Seven days for the altar and seven for the feast, and then a day to close it. Nobody was in a hurry, and the whole country was there from one end of the land to the other.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Solomon held the feast for seven days, and all Israel with him, a very great assembly, from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt. And on the eighth day they held a solemn assembly, for they had kept the dedication of the altar seven days and the feast seven days. On the twenty-third day of the seventh month he sent the people away to their homes, joyful and glad of heart for the prosperity that the LORD had granted to David and to Solomon and to Israel his people. Thus Solomon finished the house of the LORD and the king's house. All that Solomon had planned to do in the house of the LORD and in his own house he successfully accomplished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The feast runs seven days, and the assembly is described by its edges: from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt. The northern pass and the southern wadi — the whole territory, end to end, the same span the Chronicler used when David first went to fetch the ark.

Then the arithmetic of the fortnight. Seven days for the dedication of the altar and seven days for the feast of Tabernacles, and on the eighth day a solemn assembly to close it. Two full weeks, and nobody hurried.

On the twenty-third day of the seventh month he sent the people away to their homes, joyful and glad of heart for the prosperity that the LORD had granted to David and to Solomon and to Israel his people.

Three names in that clause, and the first of them has been dead for years. The gladness is for what God granted to David and to Solomon and to Israel, in that order, and the man who bought the ground and gathered the gold and drew the plans is named first at the dedication he never saw.

Then the project is signed off: Thus Solomon finished the house of the LORD and the king's house. Both again, as in the first verse of chapter 2. The Chronicler will not separate them and will not comment on them, and a reader who knows how long each took can make of it what he likes.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God appears again by night. I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice (v. 12). Then he takes responsibility for the very disasters Solomon had prayed about — when I shut up the heavens ... or command the locust ... or send pestilence (v. 13) — and gives the sentence the whole book is built on: if my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land (v. 14). And he grants what Solomon asked, with something added: my eyes will be open and my ears attentive (v. 15), and my eyes and my heart will be there for all time (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 is the part that gets left off. Before the promise there is a claim: the drought and the locust and the plague are God's own doing, named in the first person. The invitation of verse 14 is extended by the one who sent the trouble it answers.
verseByVerse.examples: Solomon asked for eyes and ears. God gives eyes and ears, and then says heart — a word that was not requested and could not have been.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD appeared to Solomon in the night and said to him: "I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the LORD appeared to Solomon in the night and said to him: I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice.

Twice now God has come to this man at night — once at Gibeon before anything was built, and now with the building full of smoke. The first time he asked a question. This time he answers one.

I have heard your prayer. Solomon had asked, seven times over, that God would hear from heaven. The reply uses his word.

And then God names the building, and the name he gives it is not palace or sanctuary or dwelling. A house of sacrifice.

Solomon had said the same thing in the letter that ordered the timber, before a stone was cut: who am I to build a house for him, except as a place to make offerings before him? He had it right, and God confirms it in his own words. The most beautiful building in the ancient Near East is, by the owner's own description, a place where things are killed.

Which is what the hill had been from the beginning. A ram in a thicket, a plague stopped at a threshing floor, and now a house built over the spot with an altar in the middle of it that was too small for the first day's work.

verseByVerse.quote: When I shut up the heavens so that there is no rain, or command the locust to devour the land, or send pestilence among my people, if my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the sentence this whole book is built on — and it has a first half that usually gets left off.

When I shut up the heavens so that there is no rain, or command the locust to devour the land, or send pestilence among my people ...

Three disasters, and God claims all three in the first person. I shut up. I command. I send. There is no suggestion that the drought is bad luck, or that the locust is a natural cycle God happens to be able to work with. He says he does it.

And notice which three he picks. Solomon had prayed through seven cases, and the third was drought and the fourth was famine and locust and pestilence. God answers by quoting his own petitioner back to him. You asked me about the shut sky and the insects and the sickness; here is what I will do about them.

Then the promise. If my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land.

Four things are asked of the people and three are promised by God, and every one of the seven is a verb.

Humble themselves comes first, and it is the word this book will not let go of. It is used of Rehoboam and his princes when the Egyptians come, and of Hezekiah after his heart was proud, and of Josiah when the book was read to him — and most astonishingly of Manasseh, in irons in Babylon, who had filled Jerusalem with innocent blood and who humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers and was heard. It is also the word used of the last king of Judah, of whom it is said that he did not humble himself. The whole history from here to the exile is sorted by that verb.

Pray, and then seek my face. That is the word the previous book carried from Saul's obituary to David's last charge, and here it arrives in its plainest form. Not seek help, or seek an outcome, or seek the ark. Seek my face — which is what David told the nation to do on the day the ark came home and the thing had already been found.

And turn from their wicked ways. The fourth verb keeps the other three honest. It is possible to be humbled by circumstances, to pray hard, and to want God very much, and to change nothing. This clause is why the previous three are not a technique.

Then God's three: hear, forgive, heal. Forgiveness comes before healing, and the land is healed last. Solomon had asked for rain; God says he will deal with the sin first and the weather afterwards.

One thing has to be said plainly, because this verse is quoted more often than almost any other and usually with a nation in mind that is not this one. My people who are called by my name means, in the Hebrew, those over whom my name has been called — the covenant people, addressed at a temple God had just chosen, about a land he had given them by oath. It is not a formula for any country that would like better harvests. What does carry over is the people: those over whom his name is now called, who were bought at a price and are called by it. The promise belongs to them, and the four verbs are the same four.

verseByVerse.quote: Now my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to the prayer that is made in this place. For now I have chosen and consecrated this house that my name may be there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to the prayer that is made in this place.

Go back one chapter and find what Solomon actually asked for. His last request before the psalm was: let your eyes be open and your ears attentive to the prayer of this place. God gives it back to him word for word. Eyes open, ears attentive, this place. Nothing added, nothing trimmed — the request granted in its own vocabulary.

Then verse 16, and God does add something.

For now I have chosen and consecrated this house that my name may be there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time.

Solomon asked for eyes and ears. God says eyes and heart.
