And the priests and the Levites who were in all Israel presented themselves to him from all places where they lived. For the Levites left their common lands and their holdings and came to Judah and Jerusalem, because Jeroboam and his sons cast them out from serving as priests of the LORD.

Jeroboam had a political problem: if his people kept going up to Jerusalem three times a year, the northern kingdom would not last a generation. So he made two calves and set up his own shrines and installed his own clergy — for the high places and for the goat idols and for the calves that he had made — and put the Levites out.

They went. The law had given the tribe of Levi no territory but pasturelands and holdings attached to their towns, and that was everything they had; and rather than serve at a golden calf they walked away from it and turned up in Judah with nothing.

Then verse 16, which is the sentence to carry out of the chapter.

And those who had set their hearts to seek the LORD God of Israel came after them from all the tribes of Israel to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the LORD, the God of their fathers.

Not clergy. Farmers and traders and families from every tribe in the north, who had lost no office and had no professional stake in the argument, and who emigrated because the worship of God had been moved somewhere they could not follow. The phrase used of them is the book's own word: they had set their hearts to seek the LORD. It is the verb of Saul's obituary and David's charge and the promise in chapter 7, and here it describes ordinary people packing up a house.

And then a clock starts. They strengthened the kingdom of Judah, and for three years they made Rehoboam the son of Solomon secure, for they walked for three years in the way of David and Solomon.

Three years, said twice in one verse. The Chronicler is not describing a reign; he is timing one. The next chapter opens with the words when the rule of Rehoboam was established and he was strong, he abandoned the law of the LORD, and the three good years are being counted so that the reader knows exactly how long it lasted.

verseByVerse.quote: Rehoboam took as wife Mahalath the daughter of Jerimoth the son of David, and of Abihail the daughter of Eliab the son of Jesse, and she bore him sons, Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham. After her he took Maacah the daughter of Absalom, who bore him Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith. Rehoboam loved Maacah the daughter of Absalom above all his wives and concubines (he took eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and fathered twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters). And Rehoboam appointed Abijah the son of Maacah as chief prince among his brothers, for he intended to make him king. And he dealt wisely and distributed some of his sons through all the districts of Judah and Benjamin, in all the fortified cities, and he gave them abundant provisions and procured wives for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The household is set out last, and the arithmetic tells its own story: eighteen wives, sixty concubines, twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters.

The law of the king had named three things a king was not to multiply — horses, wives, and silver and gold. His father broke the first and the third in the chapters this book prints, and the second in the chapter it does not. The son takes up the second, and the Chronicler simply gives the numbers.

One name in the list is worth a look. Maacah the daughter of Absalom, whom Rehoboam loved above all his wives — a descendant of the son who stole his father's kingdom and died hanging in an oak. The house of David is intermarrying with its own wreckage.

And she gets what she wants. Rehoboam appointed Abijah the son of Maacah as chief prince among his brothers, for he intended to make him king — though the firstborn was Jeush, by another wife, four verses earlier. The succession goes to the favourite's son, and the Chronicler notes it without comment, as he noted the Levite who made a younger son chief because his father preferred him.

The last verse is a compliment of a sort: and he dealt wisely and distributed some of his sons through all the districts of Judah and Benjamin, in all the fortified cities, and he gave them abundant provisions and procured wives for them. It is shrewd. Scattering the princes keeps any one of them from building a base at court, and ties every garrison town to the family.

So the man is capable. He fortified well, he governed sensibly, and when a prophet told him to disband an army he disbanded it. What the next chapter reports is not incompetence. It is what happens to a competent man once he is secure.

11.theology:
God takes responsibility for the division to the face of the man who lost by it: this thing is from me. Rehoboam is not told he was wronged and should be gracious. He is told the catastrophe is God's — and the men on the other side of it are called your relatives before a sword is drawn. He listened, and sent a hundred and eighty thousand men home.

Verse 16 puts the book's governing verb into the mouths of ordinary people. Those who had set their hearts to seek the LORD came from every tribe — not clergy who had lost their posts, but families with no professional stake, who moved country because the worship of God had been relocated somewhere they could not follow.
11.examples:
The Levites walked away from the only property their tribe was allowed to own rather than serve at a golden calf, and arrived in Judah with nothing.

Verse 17 says three years twice in one sentence. The Chronicler is not describing the reign; he is timing it, so that when the next chapter opens on a king who was established and strong and abandoned the law, the reader knows exactly how long the good part lasted.

He fortified well, governed shrewdly, and disbanded an army because a prophet told him to. What follows is not the collapse of an incompetent man. It is what happened to a capable one once he was secure.

12.title: He Abandoned the Law of the LORD
12.text: <sup>1</sup>When the rule of Rehoboam was established and he was strong, he abandoned the law of the LORD, and all Israel with him.<sup>2</sup>In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, because they had been unfaithful to the LORD, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem<sup>3</sup>with 1,200 chariots and 60,000 horsemen. And the people were without number who came with him from Egypt— Libyans, Sukkiim, and Ethiopians.<sup>4</sup>And he took the fortified cities of Judah and came as far as Jerusalem.<sup>5</sup>Then Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam and to the princes of Judah, who had gathered at Jerusalem because of Shishak, and said to them, "Thus says the LORD, 'You abandoned me, so I have abandoned you to the hand of Shishak.'"<sup>6</sup>Then the princes of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, "The LORD is righteous."<sup>7</sup>When the LORD saw that they humbled themselves, the word of the LORD came to Shemaiah: "They have humbled themselves. I will not destroy them, but I will grant them some deliverance, and my wrath shall not be poured out on Jerusalem by the hand of Shishak.<sup>8</sup>Nevertheless, they shall be servants to him, that they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms of the countries."<sup>9</sup>So Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem. He took away the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house. He took away everything. He also took away the shields of gold that Solomon had made,<sup>10</sup>and King Rehoboam made in their place shields of bronze and committed them to the hands of the officers of the guard, who kept the door of the king's house.<sup>11</sup>And as often as the king went into the house of the LORD, the guard came and carried them and brought them back to the guardroom.<sup>12</sup>And when he humbled himself the wrath of the LORD turned from him, so as not to make a complete destruction. Moreover, conditions were good in Judah.<sup>13</sup>So King Rehoboam grew strong in Jerusalem and reigned. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city that the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel to put his name there. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite.<sup>14</sup>And he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.<sup>15</sup>Now the acts of Rehoboam, from first to last, are they not written in the chronicles of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer? There were continual wars between Rehoboam and Jeroboam.<sup>16</sup>And Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David, and Abijah his son reigned in his place.
12.overview:
Three years of security are enough: when the rule of Rehoboam was established and he was strong, he abandoned the law of the LORD, and all Israel with him (v. 1). Shishak of Egypt takes the fortified cities and reaches Jerusalem (vv. 2-4). Shemaiah delivers a sentence in the shape of an equation — you abandoned me, so I have abandoned you — and the king and princes humble themselves and say the LORD is righteous (vv. 5-6). God grants some deliverance and leaves them under Egypt to learn the difference between two masters (vv. 7-8). Everything is carried off, including Solomon's gold shields, and bronze copies are kept under guard (vv. 9-11). The reign closes with the verdict: he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the LORD (vv. 12-16).

The good years lasted exactly as long as the danger did. Security, not adversity, is what verse 1 names as the cause.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Established, and Strong, and Gone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the rule of Rehoboam was established and he was strong, he abandoned the law of the LORD, and all Israel with him (v. 1). In the fifth year, because they had been unfaithful to the LORD, Shishak of Egypt comes up with 1,200 chariots and 60,000 horsemen and takes the fortified cities (vv. 2-4). Shemaiah brings the sentence: You abandoned me, so I have abandoned you to the hand of Shishak (v. 5). And the princes and the king humbled themselves and said, The LORD is righteous (v. 6). God relents — I will grant them some deliverance — but leaves them as Shishak's servants that they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms of the countries (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 6 is the first time anyone in this book does what chapter 7 asked for. They humble themselves, and what they say is not a plea for mercy but a verdict on themselves: the LORD is righteous. Three words, and God moves at once.
verseByVerse.examples: The deliverance granted is some. The humbling was real and God says so, and the Egyptians still walked into Jerusalem and emptied it. Mercy did not cancel the consequence.

verseByVerse.quote: When the rule of Rehoboam was established and he was strong, he abandoned the law of the LORD, and all Israel with him. In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, because they had been unfaithful to the LORD, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem with 1,200 chariots and 60,000 horsemen. And the people were without number who came with him from Egypt— Libyans, Sukkiim, and Ethiopians. And he took the fortified cities of Judah and came as far as Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the rule of Rehoboam was established and he was strong, he abandoned the law of the LORD, and all Israel with him.

The previous chapter said three years twice in a single verse, and this is what it was counting to. The good period lasted exactly as long as the insecurity did.

Notice the two words that trigger the sentence. Established, and strong. Not corrupted, not tempted, not besieged — secure. While the throne was shaky he listened to a prophet and disbanded an army and fortified his cities and welcomed refugee Levites. The moment nothing was threatening him he abandoned the law.

And the clause at the end will not let it be a private failure: and all Israel with him. A king does not lapse alone. Whatever he stops doing, a nation stops doing.

Verse 2 gives the reason for what follows in one word: because they had been unfaithful to the LORD. The Hebrew is the verb the previous book was built on — the one used of Achan taking the devoted thing, of the tribes across the Jordan, of Judah carried to Babylon, and of Saul, who died for his breach of faith. It has crossed into this book, and it is now being used of a son of David five years into his reign.

What comes is enormous: twelve hundred chariots, sixty thousand horsemen, Libyans and Sukkiim and Ethiopians without number. The fifteen fortified cities of chapter 11 fall, all of them, and the army arrives at Jerusalem. Rehoboam had walled the right frontier and it made no difference, because the wall was never the thing that was protecting him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam and to the princes of Judah, who had gathered at Jerusalem because of Shishak, and said to them, "Thus says the LORD, 'You abandoned me, so I have abandoned you to the hand of Shishak.'" Then the princes of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, "The LORD is righteous." When the LORD saw that they humbled themselves, the word of the LORD came to Shemaiah: "They have humbled themselves. I will not destroy them, but I will grant them some deliverance, and my wrath shall not be poured out on Jerusalem by the hand of Shishak. Nevertheless, they shall be servants to him, that they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms of the countries."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shemaiah comes back. He is the prophet who stopped a civil war with three sentences in chapter 11, and the king listened to him then. Now he walks into a room where the king and the princes have gathered because there is an Egyptian army outside, and delivers a sentence with the symmetry of an equation.

You abandoned me, so I have abandoned you to the hand of Shishak.

The same verb, twice, with the subjects swapped. It is the word from verse 1 — he abandoned the law of the LORD — turned round and handed back. There is no elaboration and no argument. God simply describes the shape of what has happened.

Then comes the thing that makes this chapter matter.

Then the princes of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, The LORD is righteous.

That verb is the first one in the promise of chapter 7 — if my people who are called by my name humble themselves. This is its first appearance in the book since God spoke it, and it is the word the whole history from here to the exile will be sorted by.

Look at what they actually say. Not have mercy on us. Not we are sorry. The LORD is righteous — a verdict, delivered by the guilty party, in favour of the judge. They agree with the sentence before asking for anything, and in fact they never get round to asking for anything at all.

God moves immediately. When the LORD saw that they humbled themselves — he is watching for it — the word comes back to Shemaiah: they have humbled themselves, I will not destroy them.

But read the next clause carefully, because it is the honest part. I will grant them some deliverance. Some. The wrath will not be poured out, the city will not fall, and the Egyptians are still coming through the gate. Humbling was real and God said so and answered it, and the consequence was reduced rather than cancelled.

And verse 8 gives the reason for the part that was not cancelled. Nevertheless, they shall be servants to him, that they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms of the countries.

They will spend a season as somebody else's subjects so that they can compare. Judah has been serving God carelessly and had begun to think it a burden; a year under Egyptian taxation will teach the difference between the two masters faster than a sermon could. The consequence is not punishment left running out of severity. It is instruction.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Shishak took away everything, including the gold shields Solomon had made, and Rehoboam made in their place shields of bronze and gave them to the guard, who fetched them out whenever the king went up to the house of the LORD and carried them back to the guardroom afterwards (vv. 9-11). Because he humbled himself the wrath turned away, and conditions were good in Judah (v. 12). He reigns seventeen years in the city that the LORD had chosen; his mother was Naamah the Ammonite (v. 13). And the verdict: he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the LORD (v. 14). The sources are Shemaiah and Iddo, and the wars with Jeroboam never stopped (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 14 is the reversal of a sentence one chapter back. People from every tribe in the north had set their hearts to seek the LORD and left their homes to do it. The king they came to did not set his heart to seek him, and that is the whole indictment.
verseByVerse.examples: The bronze shields had to be carried out for ceremonies and locked up again. Gold shields hang on a wall; copies get kept in a cupboard, and somebody has to remember to bring them.

verseByVerse.quote: So Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem. He took away the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house. He took away everything. He also took away the shields of gold that Solomon had made, and King Rehoboam made in their place shields of bronze and committed them to the hands of the officers of the guard, who kept the door of the king's house. And as often as the king went into the house of the LORD, the guard came and carried them and brought them back to the guardroom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He took away the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house. He took away everything.

Everything. The stores David spent a lifetime gathering out of Edom and Moab and Ammon and Philistia and Amalek and set apart rather than spend; the gold of Ophir out of an old man's private fortune; the dedicated gifts kept under a Levite's care with Samuel's and Abner's and Joab's names still on them. Five years after Solomon's death an Egyptian carried it out of the gate.

Now the detail the Chronicler chooses to dwell on, out of all that loss.

He also took away the shields of gold that Solomon had made, and King Rehoboam made in their place shields of bronze and committed them to the hands of the officers of the guard, who kept the door of the king's house.

Five hundred shields of beaten gold had hung in the House of the Forest of Lebanon, made to be looked at, in a reign where silver was not considered as anything. The replacements are bronze.

And verse 11 is the sentence that finishes it. As often as the king went into the house of the LORD, the guard came and carried them and brought them back to the guardroom.

The gold ones hung on a wall. The bronze ones are kept locked up and fetched out for ceremonies, carried in front of the king on the way to the temple and taken straight back to the guardroom afterwards. Nobody is allowed to look at them for long.

It is one of the most exact pictures of decline in Scripture, and it is made entirely out of an administrative arrangement. The form is kept perfectly. The procession still goes up. What is being carried has been quietly substituted, and everyone concerned has agreed not to mention it.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he humbled himself the wrath of the LORD turned from him, so as not to make a complete destruction. Moreover, conditions were good in Judah. So King Rehoboam grew strong in Jerusalem and reigned. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city that the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel to put his name there. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite. And he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the LORD. Now the acts of Rehoboam, from first to last, are they not written in the chronicles of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer? There were continual wars between Rehoboam and Jeroboam. And Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David, and Abijah his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he humbled himself the wrath of the LORD turned from him, so as not to make a complete destruction. Moreover, conditions were good in Judah.

The verb again. It is used of him twice in this chapter, and both times God responds to it. Whatever else is true of Rehoboam, when he was told the truth he agreed with it — and the last clause of the verse says the country recovered. There were good things in Judah, after an invasion that took everything.

Then the summary of the reign, and two facts are laid side by side without a word joining them. He reigned seventeen years in the city that the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel to put his name there. And: his mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite.

The chosen city, and an Ammonite queen mother. Solomon's foreign marriages are not narrated in this book, and here is one of them sitting in the royal nursery producing the next king of Judah. The Chronicler does not connect the two clauses. He puts them in the same verse.

Then the verdict, and it cuts.

And he did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.

Go back one chapter. When Jeroboam threw the Levites out, people came south from every tribe in Israel — farmers and families with no office to lose — and the phrase used of them was that they had set their hearts to seek the LORD God of Israel. They left land and houses to do it.

They arrived in Judah and put themselves under a king who did not set his heart to seek him. Same words, opposite subjects, one chapter apart.

Notice too what the verdict does not say. It does not say he worshipped other gods, or murdered anybody, or robbed the temple. The charge is an omission located in the heart: he never set it. He humbled himself when the Egyptians came and agreed that God was righteous and got the wrath turned away, and he still went to his grave with the whole of him never having been pointed in one direction.

12.theology:
Verse 6 is the first time in this book that anyone does what 7:14 asked. They humble themselves — the verb the whole history from here to the exile is sorted by — and what they say is not a plea but a verdict in God's favour: the LORD is righteous. God answers at once, and the answer is honest about its limits. He grants some deliverance; the city stands and the Egyptians still empty it. And verse 8 gives his reason for the part he does not cancel — a season under another master, so that Judah can compare the two kinds of service.

Verse 14's indictment is not idolatry or violence but an omission in the heart: he did not set his heart to seek the LORD. One chapter earlier the same phrase described people who left their homes in the north because they had set their hearts to seek him. They emigrated to live under a king who never did.
12.examples:
The bronze shields had to be fetched from the guardroom for every procession and carried straight back. The form was kept perfectly, the route was unchanged, and what was being carried had been quietly substituted — which is a more exact picture of decline than any sermon about it.

What triggered the collapse was not pressure. It was the removal of pressure. While the throne was shaky Rehoboam obeyed a prophet, fortified his cities and took in refugees; the moment he was established and strong, he abandoned the law.

He humbled himself and God turned the wrath away, twice, and the epitaph still reads that he did evil. A man can respond rightly to a crisis and never once set his heart in the direction the crisis pointed.

13.title: We Have Not Abandoned the LORD
13.text: <sup>1</sup>In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam, Abijah began to reign over Judah.<sup>2</sup>He reigned for three years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Micaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. Now there was war between Abijah and Jeroboam.<sup>3</sup>Abijah went out to battle, having an army of valiant men of war, 400,000 chosen men. And Jeroboam drew up his line of battle against him with 800,000 chosen mighty warriors.<sup>4</sup>Then Abijah stood up on Mount Zemaraim that is in the hill country of Ephraim and said, "Hear me, O Jeroboam and all Israel!<sup>5</sup>Ought you not to know that the LORD God of Israel gave the kingship over Israel forever to David and his sons by a covenant of salt?<sup>6</sup>Yet Jeroboam the son of Nebat, a servant of Solomon the son of David, rose up and rebelled against his lord,<sup>7</sup>and certain worthless scoundrels gathered about him and defied Rehoboam the son of Solomon, when Rehoboam was young and irresolute and could not withstand them.<sup>8</sup>"And now you think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD in the hand of the sons of David, because you are a great multitude and have with you the golden calves that Jeroboam made you for gods.<sup>9</sup>Have you not driven out the priests of the LORD, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and made priests for yourselves like the peoples of other lands? Whoever comes for ordination with a young bull or seven rams becomes a priest of what are not gods.<sup>10</sup>But as for us, the LORD is our God, and we have not forsaken him. We have priests ministering to the LORD who are sons of Aaron, and Levites for their service.<sup>11</sup>They offer to the LORD every morning and every evening burnt offerings and incense of sweet spices, set out the showbread on the table of pure gold, and care for the golden lampstand that its lamps may burn every evening. For we keep the charge of the LORD our God, but you have forsaken him.<sup>12</sup>Behold, God is with us at our head, and his priests with their battle trumpets to sound the call to battle against you. O sons of Israel, do not fight against the LORD, the God of your fathers, for you cannot succeed."<sup>13</sup>Jeroboam had sent an ambush around to come upon them from behind. Thus his troops were in front of Judah, and the ambush was behind them.<sup>14</sup>And when Judah looked, behold, the battle was in front of and behind them. And they cried to the LORD, and the priests blew the trumpets.<sup>15</sup>Then the men of Judah raised the battle shout. And when the men of Judah shouted, God defeated Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah.<sup>16</sup>The men of Israel fled before Judah, and God gave them into their hand.<sup>17</sup>Abijah and his people struck them with great force, so there fell slain of Israel 500,000 chosen men.<sup>18</sup>Thus the men of Israel were subdued at that time, and the men of Judah prevailed, because they relied on the LORD, the God of their fathers.<sup>19</sup>And Abijah pursued Jeroboam and took cities from him, Bethel with its villages and Jeshanah with its villages and Ephron with its villages.<sup>20</sup>Jeroboam did not recover his power in the days of Abijah. And the LORD struck him down, and he died.<sup>21</sup>But Abijah grew mighty. And he took fourteen wives and had twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.<sup>22</sup>The rest of the acts of Abijah, his ways and his sayings, are written in the story of the prophet Iddo.
13.overview:
Abijah goes to war outnumbered two to one, climbs a hill in enemy territory, and preaches at the opposing army (vv. 1-4). His case: the throne was given to David's sons by a covenant of salt, Jeroboam rebelled, and the north is now proposing to fight the kingdom of the LORD with a multitude, two golden calves and a priesthood any man can buy with a bull and seven rams (vv. 5-9). Judah's evidence is the daily service — offerings morning and evening, the bread set out, the lamps lit (vv. 10-11) — and his last word is an appeal to call the battle off (v. 12). Jeroboam ambushes him from behind; Judah cries out, the priests blow the trumpets, and God defeats Israel (vv. 13-18). Jeroboam never recovers (vv. 19-22).

The whole episode is Chronicles' own; Kings gives Abijam three verses and a bad verdict. Both stand, and the chapter itself supplies the tension — he preaches in verse 11 and takes fourteen wives in verse 21.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — A Sermon on a Mountain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abijah reigns three years and goes to war outnumbered two to one — 400,000 against 800,000 (vv. 1-3). He climbs Mount Zemaraim and preaches. The kingship was given to David and his sons by a covenant of salt (vv. 4-5); Jeroboam was Solomon's servant and rebelled while Rehoboam was young and irresolute (vv. 6-7); and the north now proposes to withstand the kingdom of the LORD in the hand of the sons of David with a multitude and two golden calves (v. 8). Their priesthood is for sale to anyone with a bull and seven rams (v. 9). But as for us, the LORD is our God, and we have not forsaken him (v. 10) — and the evidence offered is the daily service (v. 11). Do not fight against the LORD, the God of your fathers, for you cannot succeed (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Abijah's argument for Judah is not its army or its capital or its king. It is that the morning and evening offerings are still being made, the bread is still being set out, and the lamps are still lit. He rests a nation's legitimacy on a routine.
verseByVerse.examples: Every word of the sermon is true and the man preaching it is given three verses and a bad verdict in the book of Kings. Both accounts stand. A person can state the case for God accurately in public and not live inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam, Abijah began to reign over Judah. He reigned for three years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Micaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. Now there was war between Abijah and Jeroboam. Abijah went out to battle, having an army of valiant men of war, 400,000 chosen men. And Jeroboam drew up his line of battle against him with 800,000 chosen mighty warriors. Then Abijah stood up on Mount Zemaraim that is in the hill country of Ephraim and said, "Hear me, O Jeroboam and all Israel!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abijah gets three years and a battle. His mother is named as Micaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah, where the previous chapter called her Maacah the daughter of Absalom; the usual reconciliation is that she was Absalom's granddaughter through his daughter Tamar, who married Uriel, and that both names belonged to her. It cannot be settled and nothing depends on it.

The armies are given as four hundred thousand against eight hundred thousand. Whatever the figures represent, the ratio is the point: Judah is outnumbered two to one and both sides know it.

Then Abijah does something no other king in this book does. Abijah stood up on Mount Zemaraim that is in the hill country of Ephraim and said, Hear me, O Jeroboam and all Israel!

He is standing on northern soil, in Ephraim, in front of an army twice the size of his own, and instead of a battle speech to his own men he preaches at the enemy. What follows is eight verses of theology delivered across a valley to people who have come to kill him.

verseByVerse.quote: Ought you not to know that the LORD God of Israel gave the kingship over Israel forever to David and his sons by a covenant of salt? Yet Jeroboam the son of Nebat, a servant of Solomon the son of David, rose up and rebelled against his lord, and certain worthless scoundrels gathered about him and defied Rehoboam the son of Solomon, when Rehoboam was young and irresolute and could not withstand them. "And now you think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD in the hand of the sons of David, because you are a great multitude and have with you the golden calves that Jeroboam made you for gods. Have you not driven out the priests of the LORD, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and made priests for yourselves like the peoples of other lands? Whoever comes for ordination with a young bull or seven rams becomes a priest of what are not gods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The case opens with a covenant. Ought you not to know that the LORD God of Israel gave the kingship over Israel forever to David and his sons by a covenant of salt?

A covenant of salt is a phrase from the law, used of the priests' portion and of the grain offering, and the image is preservation: salt is what keeps a thing from going off. A covenant of salt is one that does not spoil with time. Abijah is not claiming his family deserves the throne. He is claiming that God said something and that the saying has not gone stale.

Then the history, and it is partisan but not false. Jeroboam was a servant of Solomon the son of David who rose up and rebelled against his lord, and worthless men gathered round him when Rehoboam was young and irresolute and could not withstand them. Rehoboam was forty-one at the time, so young is a kindness; irresolute is not.

And then the charge that matters. And now you think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD in the hand of the sons of David.

The kingdom of the LORD. That is what the previous book called it three times — my house and my kingdom, the throne of the kingdom of the LORD, Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD — and here a king of Judah says it out loud to an opposing army. He is not defending a dynasty. He is telling them whose chair they are attacking.

Against which the north has two assets, and Abijah names both with contempt: you are a great multitude, and you have with you the golden calves that Jeroboam made you for gods. Numbers, and manufactured deities.

Then the priesthood, and the sentence is devastating: whoever comes for ordination with a young bull or seven rams becomes a priest of what are not gods. The north has made ordination a transaction — bring the livestock and you are a priest — and Abijah adds the clause that finishes it: a priest of things that are not gods. A real fee, a real ceremony, a real title, and nothing at the other end of it.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for us, the LORD is our God, and we have not forsaken him. We have priests ministering to the LORD who are sons of Aaron, and Levites for their service. They offer to the LORD every morning and every evening burnt offerings and incense of sweet spices, set out the showbread on the table of pure gold, and care for the golden lampstand that its lamps may burn every evening. For we keep the charge of the LORD our God, but you have forsaken him. Behold, God is with us at our head, and his priests with their battle trumpets to sound the call to battle against you. O sons of Israel, do not fight against the LORD, the God of your fathers, for you cannot succeed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the positive case, and it is the reason this speech is in Scripture.

But as for us, the LORD is our God, and we have not forsaken him.

Then the evidence — and a modern reader braced for a claim about armies or righteousness or the temple's magnificence gets none of it.

We have priests ministering to the LORD who are sons of Aaron, and Levites for their service. They offer to the LORD every morning and every evening burnt offerings and incense of sweet spices, set out the showbread on the table of pure gold, and care for the golden lampstand that its lamps may burn every evening. For we keep the charge of the LORD our God, but you have forsaken him.

That is the whole argument. The right men are doing the right things at the right hours. Somebody lights the lamps every evening. Somebody puts fresh bread on the table. The sacrifice goes up at dawn and again at dusk, and it went up yesterday and will go up tomorrow.

He rests the legitimacy of a kingdom on a routine — the very thing the Chronicler reported in one flat sentence at the end of Solomon's building programme, that they did not turn aside from what the king had commanded. Nobody writes ballads about the evening lamp. It is what a nation has left when everything interesting about it has gone, and it turns out to be what a nation is.

Then the summons: Behold, God is with us at our head, and his priests with their battle trumpets to sound the call to battle against you. O sons of Israel, do not fight against the LORD, the God of your fathers, for you cannot succeed.

He calls them sons of Israel and names God as the God of your fathers. Standing in front of an army he is about to fight, he will not concede that they are not family or that God is not theirs. His last word before the trumpets is an appeal to call it off.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — The Trumpets, and the Shout
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeroboam has sent an ambush round behind, so that the battle was in front of and behind them (vv. 13-14a). Judah's response is two things at once: they cried to the LORD, and the priests blew the trumpets, and the men raised the battle shout (vv. 14b-15). God defeats Jeroboam; Israel flees and half a million fall (vv. 15-17). The men of Judah prevailed, because they relied on the LORD, the God of their fathers (v. 18). Abijah takes Bethel and other towns, Jeroboam never recovers, and the LORD strikes him down (vv. 19-20). Abijah grows mighty, takes fourteen wives, and his acts are written in the story of Iddo (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The trumpets are not morale. The law had said that when Israel went to war it should sound an alarm with the trumpets so as to be remembered before the LORD and saved from its enemies. Surrounded, the priests do exactly what was written, and the text says God defeated Jeroboam.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 18 gives the reason in one word: they leaned on him. Three chapters from now a different king of Judah will lean on Syria instead, and a seer will use this same verb against him.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeroboam had sent an ambush around to come upon them from behind. Thus his troops were in front of Judah, and the ambush was behind them. And when Judah looked, behold, the battle was in front of and behind them. And they cried to the LORD, and the priests blew the trumpets. Then the men of Judah raised the battle shout. And when the men of Judah shouted, God defeated Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah. The men of Israel fled before Judah, and God gave them into their hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They do not call it off. And while Abijah has been preaching, Jeroboam has been moving.

Jeroboam had sent an ambush around to come upon them from behind. Thus his troops were in front of Judah, and the ambush was behind them.

The sermon has been answered with a manoeuvre. While the king of Judah was talking about covenants of salt, half of the northern army was walking round the back of the hill.

The text lets them see it: when Judah looked, behold, the battle was in front of and behind them. Outnumbered two to one and now surrounded, on ground that is not theirs.

What they do next is two things in one verse, and the order is not the natural one. And they cried to the LORD, and the priests blew the trumpets. Then the men of Judah raised the battle shout.

The trumpets are not a morale device and they are not a signal. The law had given an instruction about them: when you go to war in your land against the adversary who oppresses you, then you shall sound an alarm with the trumpets, that you may be remembered before the LORD your God and be saved from your enemies. Surrounded on a hillside in Ephraim, the priests do exactly what was written down for exactly this situation.

And the next clause does not say the men of Judah broke out. God defeated Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah. The subject of the verb is God. They cried, they blew, they shouted, and somebody else won it.

verseByVerse.quote: Abijah and his people struck them with great force, so there fell slain of Israel 500,000 chosen men. Thus the men of Israel were subdued at that time, and the men of Judah prevailed, because they relied on the LORD, the God of their fathers. And Abijah pursued Jeroboam and took cities from him, Bethel with its villages and Jeshanah with its villages and Ephron with its villages. Jeroboam did not recover his power in the days of Abijah. And the LORD struck him down, and he died. But Abijah grew mighty. And he took fourteen wives and had twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters. The rest of the acts of Abijah, his ways and his sayings, are written in the story of the prophet Iddo.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The slaughter is enormous — half a million, which is more than the whole of Jeroboam's line of battle in verse 3 if the figures are read as we would read them. The Hebrew word behind a thousand can also mean a unit or a contingent, and that may account for the scale here and elsewhere in these books. The Chronicler is reporting a rout of a kind nobody expected, and the arithmetic should not be allowed to become the subject.

The reason is given in verse 18, and it is one word. Thus the men of Israel were subdued at that time, and the men of Judah prevailed, because they relied on the LORD, the God of their fathers.

Relied is a verb meaning to lean your weight on something. Judah was outnumbered, outmanoeuvred and surrounded, and it put its weight on God and the thing held.

Keep the word. Three chapters from now another king of Judah will be in trouble and will send silver and gold to the king of Syria to buy an alliance, and a seer will come to him and use this same verb twice — you have leaned on the king of Syria and not on the LORD your God, and the Ethiopians were a huge army and you leaned on him then and he gave them into your hand. The word runs between the two chapters like a wire.

Abijah takes Bethel — the town with one of the calves in it — and Jeroboam did not recover his power in the days of Abijah, and the LORD struck him down and he died.

Then the last thing said about Abijah, and it is not the sermon. But Abijah grew mighty. And he took fourteen wives and had twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.

Fourteen wives. His father had eighteen and sixty concubines; his grandfather had the number this book declines to print. The man who stood on a mountain and told an army that Judah had not forsaken the LORD went home and did what the law of the king forbids, and the Chronicler records the sermon and the wives in the same chapter without reconciling them.

That has to be said plainly, because the other account of this reign is short and severe: three verses, and the judgement that he walked in all the sins of his father. Both books are telling the truth. Chronicles is not rehabilitating Abijah; it is recording that on one day, on one hill, this man said exactly the right thing about God and about the kingdom, and that God honoured what was said. A person can state the case for God accurately in public, and be right, and be heard — and still not live inside what he has just said. The sermon was true. It was not a description of him.

13.theology:
Abijah rests the legitimacy of a kingdom on a routine. Not the army, not the capital, not the king — the right men doing the right things at the right hours: burnt offerings every morning and every evening, incense, the showbread, the lamps burning every evening. For we keep the charge of the LORD our God. Nobody writes ballads about the evening lamp; it is what a nation has left when everything interesting about it has gone, and it turns out to be what the nation is.

And when Judah is surrounded, the priests blow trumpets because the law had told them to — that you may be remembered before the LORD your God and be saved from your enemies — and the text does not say Judah broke out. It says God defeated Jeroboam. Verse 18 names the reason in one verb: they leaned on him. Three chapters on, a seer will use that same verb against a king of Judah who leaned on Syria.
13.examples:
He preached at the enemy. Outnumbered two to one, standing on their ground, with an army in front of him that had come to kill him, and his last sentence before the trumpets was an appeal to call it off — addressed to them as sons of Israel, whose fathers' God he would not concede was not theirs.

The northern priesthood could be had for a bull and seven rams. A real fee, a real ceremony, a real title — and, as Abijah finishes the sentence, a priest of what are not gods.

The man who said all this correctly went home and took fourteen wives, and the other account of his reign says he walked in all his father's sins. Saying the right thing about God, in public, and being right, is not the same as living inside it.

14.title: He Sought the LORD
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Abijah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David. And Asa his son reigned in his place. In his days the land had rest for ten years.<sup>2</sup>And Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God.<sup>3</sup>He took away the foreign altars and the high places and broke down the pillars and cut down the Asherim<sup>4</sup>and commanded Judah to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, and to keep the law and the commandment.<sup>5</sup>He also took out of all the cities of Judah the high places and the incense altars. And the kingdom had rest under him.<sup>6</sup>He built fortified cities in Judah, for the land had rest. He had no war in those years, for the LORD gave him peace.<sup>7</sup>And he said to Judah, "Let us build these cities and surround them with walls and towers, gates and bars. The land is still ours, because we have sought the LORD our God. We have sought him, and he has given us peace on every side." So they built and prospered.<sup>8</sup>And Asa had an army of 300,000 from Judah, armed with large shields and spears, and 280,000 men from Benjamin that carried shields and drew bows. All these were mighty men of valor.<sup>9</sup>Zerah the Ethiopian came out against them with an army of a million men and 300 chariots, and came as far as Mareshah.<sup>10</sup>And Asa went out to meet him, and they drew up their lines of battle in the Valley of Zephathah at Mareshah.<sup>11</sup>And Asa cried to the LORD his God, "O LORD, there is none like you to help, between the mighty and the weak. Help us, O LORD our God, for we rely on you, and in your name we have come against this multitude. O LORD, you are our God; let not man prevail against you."<sup>12</sup>So the LORD defeated the Ethiopians before Asa and before Judah, and the Ethiopians fled.<sup>13</sup>Asa and the people who were with him pursued them as far as Gerar, and the Ethiopians fell until none remained alive, for they were broken before the LORD and his army. The men of Judah carried away very much spoil.<sup>14</sup>And they attacked all the cities around Gerar, for the fear of the LORD was upon them. They plundered all the cities, for there was much plunder in them.<sup>15</sup>And they struck down the tents of those who had livestock and carried away sheep in abundance and camels. Then they returned to Jerusalem.
14.overview:
Ten years of rest open the reign, and Asa spends them clearing out foreign altars, high places, pillars and Asherim, and commanding Judah to seek the LORD (vv. 1-5). He builds fortified cities because there is peace, and names the reason for the peace in his one recorded speech — we have sought him, and he has given us peace on every side (vv. 6-8). Then Zerah the Ethiopian invades with a million men, Asa prays four sentences, and the LORD defeated the Ethiopians (vv. 9-12). They are pursued to Gerar and broken before the LORD and his army, and Judah goes home loaded (vv. 13-15).

The word rest occurs four times in the first six verses. The Chronicler is establishing an interval so that the reader can see what Asa did with it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Ten Years of Rest, and What He Did With Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In his days the land had rest for ten years (v. 1), and Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God (v. 2). He clears out the foreign altars, the high places, the pillars and the Asherim, and commanded Judah to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, and to keep the law and the commandment (vv. 3-5). He uses the quiet to build: let us build these cities and surround them with walls and towers, gates and bars. The land is still ours, because we have sought the LORD our God (vv. 6-7). And he raises an army of 580,000 (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 7 has Asa naming the cause of his own good fortune, and he says the word twice in one breath: we have sought the LORD, we have sought him. The peace is not luck and he will not let it be called luck.
verseByVerse.examples: He fortified during the rest, not after it. Ten quiet years were spent putting up walls for a war that had not come, which is the only time walls can be built.

verseByVerse.quote: Abijah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David. And Asa his son reigned in his place. In his days the land had rest for ten years. And Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God. He took away the foreign altars and the high places and broke down the pillars and cut down the Asherim and commanded Judah to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, and to keep the law and the commandment. He also took out of all the cities of Judah the high places and the incense altars. And the kingdom had rest under him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A word arrives in this chapter and will not leave: rest. In his days the land had rest for ten years. It comes again in verse 5, and twice more in verse 6, and it means quiet — nothing happening, no armies on the roads.

Then the verdict, given at the front of the reign rather than the end of it: Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God.

And what that consisted of is listed, and it is all demolition. The foreign altars. The high places. The pillars broken down. The Asherim cut down. The incense altars taken out of every city in Judah. His great-grandfather had built some of these, his grandmother had commissioned one of them, and his father had preached against the northern calves while leaving the southern furniture standing.

Reform is mostly removal, and removal is unpopular in a way that building never is. Somebody had paid for each of those altars, and somebody's family had used it.

Then the positive half, and it is a command rather than a project. And commanded Judah to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, and to keep the law and the commandment.

Seek. It is the word the previous book carried from Saul's obituary to David's last charge, and it is the word God used in the promise at the dedication. Asa issues it as a royal order to a whole nation — and it will be said of him, twenty-five years and two chapters from now, that in his last illness he did not seek the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: He built fortified cities in Judah, for the land had rest. He had no war in those years, for the LORD gave him peace. And he said to Judah, "Let us build these cities and surround them with walls and towers, gates and bars. The land is still ours, because we have sought the LORD our God. We have sought him, and he has given us peace on every side." So they built and prospered. And Asa had an army of 300,000 from Judah, armed with large shields and spears, and 280,000 men from Benjamin that carried shields and drew bows. All these were mighty men of valor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He built fortified cities in Judah, for the land had rest. He had no war in those years, for the LORD gave him peace.

The logic of that sentence is the opposite of the usual one. He built because there was rest. Most people treat a quiet season as the reward and the work as what happens when trouble forces it; Asa treats the quiet as the working window, because walls cannot be raised during a siege.

And he says so out loud to the nation, in the only speech recorded of him.

Let us build these cities and surround them with walls and towers, gates and bars. The land is still ours, because we have sought the LORD our God. We have sought him, and he has given us peace on every side.

He says the verb twice in one breath. We have sought him — we have sought him — and the peace followed. He will not let the calm be explained by anything else: not the weakness of his neighbours, not the size of his army, not his own competence, all of which were available as explanations.

Then the army is counted: three hundred thousand from Judah with the heavy shield and spear, and two hundred and eighty thousand Benjaminites with the lighter shield and the bow. Five hundred and eighty thousand men, well equipped, in a fortified country, after ten years of preparation.

Which is exactly the position a man is in when he is about to find out what he has actually been trusting.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Between the Mighty and the Weak
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zerah the Ethiopian comes with a million men and three hundred chariots (v. 9), and Asa goes out to meet him and prays: O LORD, there is none like you to help, between the mighty and the weak. Help us, O LORD our God, for we rely on you, and in your name we have come against this multitude. O LORD, you are our God; let not man prevail against you (vv. 10-11). So the LORD defeated the Ethiopians before Asa and before Judah (v. 12); they are pursued to Gerar and broken before the LORD and his army (v. 13), and the surrounding towns are plundered because the fear of the LORD was upon them (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer's first line settles the arithmetic before the battle starts. There is none like God to help between the mighty and the weak — meaning the gap between a million men and five hundred thousand is not a category he works in.
verseByVerse.examples: The last clause turns the ownership of the fight over: let not man prevail against you. Not against us. Asa has understood whose battle he is standing in.

verseByVerse.quote: Zerah the Ethiopian came out against them with an army of a million men and 300 chariots, and came as far as Mareshah. And Asa went out to meet him, and they drew up their lines of battle in the Valley of Zephathah at Mareshah. And Asa cried to the LORD his God, "O LORD, there is none like you to help, between the mighty and the weak. Help us, O LORD our God, for we rely on you, and in your name we have come against this multitude. O LORD, you are our God; let not man prevail against you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zerah the Ethiopian came out against them with an army of a million men and 300 chariots.

Whatever the figure represents, the writer means an army that made Asa's five hundred and eighty thousand look thin, and it has come as far as Mareshah, inside Judah, in the lowlands.

And Asa goes out to meet it — and prays. The prayer is four sentences long and there is not a wasted word in it.

O LORD, there is none like you to help, between the mighty and the weak.

That first line disposes of the arithmetic before the battle begins. When it comes to helping, God does not operate in the space between strong and weak; the gap that is everything to a commander counting shields is not a category he works in. Asa is not asking God to make up a deficit. He is saying there is no deficit to make up.

Help us, O LORD our God, for we rely on you.

Rely is a verb meaning to lean your weight onto something. It is the word used of his father's army when they were surrounded on a hillside and the priests blew the trumpets — Judah prevailed because they relied on the LORD. Asa has learned the family vocabulary and is using it correctly, and it is the word that will be turned against him by a seer in two chapters' time.

And in your name we have come against this multitude. Not in our strength, and not in a just cause. In your name — as men sent, carrying somebody else's authority.

And then the last clause, which changes whose fight it is. O LORD, you are our God; let not man prevail against you.

Against you. Not against us. Asa has stopped asking God to defend Judah and started asking him to defend his own honour, on the ground that a defeat here would be a defeat of God rather than of a king. It is the argument Moses used at Sinai and the one David used in the valley, and it is available to anybody who is genuinely on God's business rather than his own.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD defeated the Ethiopians before Asa and before Judah, and the Ethiopians fled. Asa and the people who were with him pursued them as far as Gerar, and the Ethiopians fell until none remained alive, for they were broken before the LORD and his army. The men of Judah carried away very much spoil. And they attacked all the cities around Gerar, for the fear of the LORD was upon them. They plundered all the cities, for there was much plunder in them. And they struck down the tents of those who had livestock and carried away sheep in abundance and camels. Then they returned to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the LORD defeated the Ethiopians before Asa and before Judah, and the Ethiopians fled.

The subject of the verb is God, exactly as it was when Abijah was surrounded. Judah fought; the sentence does not say Judah won.

The pursuit runs twenty-five miles to Gerar, and the phrase used of the collapse should be kept: they were broken before the LORD and his army.

His army. Five hundred and eighty thousand men with shields and bows, mustered by a king of Judah in his own capital, and at the moment of victory the chronicle calls them God's troops. It is the same instinct that made Asa say let not man prevail against you an hour earlier, and God has evidently accepted the transfer.

Then the towns around Gerar are plundered, for the fear of the LORD was upon them — on the towns, not on Judah — and the men go home with sheep and camels in abundance.

A decade of rest, spent building. One prayer, four sentences long, offered by a man outnumbered nearly two to one. And the record does not say that Asa was brave or that his preparations paid off, both of which were true. It says the LORD defeated them.

14.theology:
Asa's prayer settles the arithmetic before the fighting starts: there is none like you to help, between the mighty and the weak. The gap that is everything to a man counting shields is not a category God works in — so the request is not that a deficit be made up but that there was never a deficit. And the last clause moves the ownership of the battle: let not man prevail against you. Not against us.

The verb in we rely on you means to lean your weight onto something. It was used of Judah surrounded on a hillside one chapter ago, and a seer will use it against this same king two chapters from now, when he leans on Syria instead. The whole Asa cycle is built on that one word.
14.examples:
He built the walls during the ten quiet years, because there is no other time walls can be built. Most people treat a calm season as the reward and the work as what trouble forces on them.

His reform was almost entirely demolition — altars, pillars, Asherim, incense stands, taken out of every city. Somebody had paid for each of them and somebody's family had used it, and removal is unpopular in a way that building never is.

He would not let the peace be explained by anything except seeking God, and said so twice in one sentence — though the weakness of his neighbours, the size of his army and his own competence were all available as explanations.

15.title: Seek Him and He Will Be Found
15.text: <sup>1</sup>The Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded,<sup>2</sup>and he went out to meet Asa and said to him, "Hear me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin: The LORD is with you while you are with him. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you.<sup>3</sup>For a long time Israel was without the true God, and without a teaching priest and without law,<sup>4</sup>but when in their distress they turned to the LORD, the God of Israel, and sought him, he was found by them.<sup>5</sup>In those times there was no peace to him who went out or to him who came in, for great disturbances afflicted all the inhabitants of the lands.<sup>6</sup>They were broken in pieces. Nation was crushed by nation and city by city, for God troubled them with every sort of distress.<sup>7</sup>But you, take courage! Do not let your hands be weak, for your work shall be rewarded."<sup>8</sup>As soon as Asa heard these words, the prophecy of Azariah the son of Oded, he took courage and put away the detestable idols from all the land of Judah and Benjamin and from the cities that he had taken in the hill country of Ephraim, and he repaired the altar of the LORD that was in front of the vestibule of the house of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>And he gathered all Judah and Benjamin, and those from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon who were residing with them, for great numbers had deserted to him from Israel when they saw that the LORD his God was with him.<sup>10</sup>They were gathered at Jerusalem in the third month of the fifteenth year of the reign of Asa.<sup>11</sup>They sacrificed to the LORD on that day from the spoil that they had brought 700 oxen and 7,000 sheep.<sup>12</sup>And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, with all their heart and with all their soul,<sup>13</sup>but that whoever would not seek the LORD, the God of Israel, should be put to death, whether young or old, man or woman.<sup>14</sup>They swore an oath to the LORD with a loud voice and with shouting and with trumpets and with horns.<sup>15</sup>And all Judah rejoiced over the oath, for they had sworn with all their heart and had sought him with their whole desire, and he was found by them, and the LORD gave them rest all around.<sup>16</sup>Even Maacah, his mother, King Asa removed from being queen mother because she had made a detestable image for Asherah. Asa cut down her image, crushed it, and burned it at the brook Kidron.<sup>17</sup>But the high places were not taken out of Israel. Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true all his days.<sup>18</sup>And he brought into the house of God the sacred gifts of his father and his own sacred gifts, silver, and gold, and vessels.<sup>19</sup>And there was no more war until the thirty-fifth year of the reign of Asa.
15.overview: Azariah meets the returning army with a word from the Spirit: if you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you — David's charge to Solomon arriving three generations later — supported by the era of the judges, when God troubled Israel until they turned and sought him (vv. 1-7). Asa takes courage, clears out the idols and repairs the neglected altar (v. 8), and gathers Judah with defectors from three northern tribes (vv. 9-11). They covenant to seek the LORD with all their heart, on pain of death, and swear it aloud with trumpets — and he was found by them (vv. 12-15). Asa then deposes his own grandmother and burns her idol at the Kidron; the high places stand, and his heart is called wholly true all his days (vv. 16-19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — If You Seek Him, He Will Be Found
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded, and he goes out to meet the returning army (v. 1). His word is a sentence with two halves: the LORD is with you while you are with him. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you (v. 2). Then a history lesson — Israel long without the true God, and without a teaching priest and without law, until in their distress they turned and sought him and he was found by them (vv. 3-4) — in an age when nobody could travel safely and God troubled them with every sort of distress (vv. 5-6). And the application: But you, take courage! Do not let your hands be weak, for your work shall be rewarded (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 2 is David's charge to Solomon, almost word for word, arriving through a prophet three generations later. What an old king said privately to his son on the day he handed over the plans is now the standing terms for every king after him.
verseByVerse.examples: The prophet's history lesson names God as the author of the distress that produced the turning. He troubled them, and in their distress they sought him and found him. The trouble was not an obstacle to the finding; it was the road to it.

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded, and he went out to meet Asa and said to him, "Hear me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin: The LORD is with you while you are with him. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you. For a long time Israel was without the true God, and without a teaching priest and without law, but when in their distress they turned to the LORD, the God of Israel, and sought him, he was found by them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The army is coming home loaded with plunder from Gerar, and a man walks out to meet them.

The Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded, and he went out to meet Asa. He is named nowhere else in Scripture. He arrives at the one moment when a victorious king is least inclined to listen to advice, and says this:

The LORD is with you while you are with him. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you.

An old man said that once before. On the day David handed Solomon the plans for the temple, in front of the whole assembly, he told his son to know the God of his father and serve him with a whole heart — if you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever.

Three generations later a prophet nobody has heard of says it back to David's great-great-grandson, almost syllable for syllable. What was spoken privately to one boy about one building has become the standing terms of the dynasty, and the Spirit of God is what brought it back.

Then Azariah gives his evidence, and it is the book of Judges. For a long time Israel was without the true God, and without a teaching priest and without law.

Three absences, and the middle one is easy to skip. Without a teaching priest. Not without priests — without any who taught. The office continued and the instruction stopped, and a nation went four centuries not knowing what it had been told, because the men whose job was to say it had found other things to do.

But when in their distress they turned to the LORD, the God of Israel, and sought him, he was found by them. That is the whole cycle of the judges in one sentence, and it is offered as proof of the promise: it has been tested, repeatedly, by people in a much worse position than Asa is in.

verseByVerse.quote: In those times there was no peace to him who went out or to him who came in, for great disturbances afflicted all the inhabitants of the lands. They were broken in pieces. Nation was crushed by nation and city by city, for God troubled them with every sort of distress. But you, take courage! Do not let your hands be weak, for your work shall be rewarded."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The description of that era is bleak and precise. In those times there was no peace to him who went out or to him who came in, for great disturbances afflicted all the inhabitants of the lands. They were broken in pieces. Nation was crushed by nation and city by city.

No safe travel. No one could leave home and expect to arrive. And the fragmentation is described twice over — nation against nation, and then city against city, which is worse, because it means the collapse had reached inside the borders.

And then the clause that explains it: for God troubled them with every sort of distress.

God did it. The prophet is not describing a period when God was absent and things fell apart; he is describing a period when God was actively making things difficult. It is the same first-person claim God made at the dedication — I shut up the heavens, I command the locust, I send pestilence — and it stands in front of the promise for the same reason. The distress that drove Israel back to him was his own instrument.

Then the application, and it is two imperatives and a promise. But you, take courage! Do not let your hands be weak, for your work shall be rewarded.

Weak hands is the Bible's picture of a person who has stopped, and the encouragement is aimed at a man in the middle of a reform that will make him unpopular. Your work shall be rewarded — literally, there is wages for what you are doing. Azariah does not tell him it will be easy or that people will thank him. He tells him it will be paid.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — A Covenant Sworn With Shouting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As soon as Asa heard these words ... he took courage, put away the detestable idols, and repaired the altar of the LORD that was in front of the vestibule (v. 8). He gathers Judah and Benjamin with those from Ephraim, Manasseh and Simeon — for great numbers had deserted to him from Israel when they saw that the LORD his God was with him (vv. 9-10). Seven hundred oxen and seven thousand sheep are sacrificed (v. 11), and they enter a covenant to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, with all their heart and with all their soul, on pain of death for refusing (vv. 12-13). They swear it aloud with trumpets and horns (v. 14), and he was found by them, and the LORD gave them rest all around (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 15 is verse 2 kept inside a single chapter. The promise was: seek him and he will be found by you. The report is: they sought him with their whole desire, and he was found by them. The Chronicler does not leave the reader to wonder whether it worked.
verseByVerse.examples: The altar had to be repaired. Sixty years after fire came down on it in front of the whole nation, the stonework had been let go. Neglect shows up first in the fabric, and somebody walked past that altar every day for a generation.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Asa heard these words, the prophecy of Azariah the son of Oded, he took courage and put away the detestable idols from all the land of Judah and Benjamin and from the cities that he had taken in the hill country of Ephraim, and he repaired the altar of the LORD that was in front of the vestibule of the house of the LORD. And he gathered all Judah and Benjamin, and those from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon who were residing with them, for great numbers had deserted to him from Israel when they saw that the LORD his God was with him. They were gathered at Jerusalem in the third month of the fifteenth year of the reign of Asa. They sacrificed to the LORD on that day from the spoil that they had brought 700 oxen and 7,000 sheep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As soon as Asa heard these words ... he took courage.

As soon as. The prophet finished and the king moved, and what he does with the courage is immediately more demolition: the detestable idols out of Judah and Benjamin, and out of the towns he had taken in Ephraim as well.

And then a small clause with a long shadow. And he repaired the altar of the LORD that was in front of the vestibule of the house of the LORD.

That altar is the one fire came down on. Solomon dedicated it in front of the whole nation, the glory filled the house, and the priests could not get in. Sixty years later it needs repointing. Nobody destroyed it and nobody moved it; the stonework was simply allowed to go, in the courtyard of a working temple, while priests walked past it every day.

Decline rarely announces itself. It shows in the fabric first, and by the time somebody notices that the altar wants repair, the noticing itself is the reform.

Then a gathering, and the guest list is unexpected: Judah and Benjamin, and those from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon who were residing with them, for great numbers had deserted to him from Israel when they saw that the LORD his God was with him.

Migration south again, as in Rehoboam's first years — and the reason given this time is not that they had been thrown out of office. They came when they saw that the LORD his God was with him. People from three northern tribes watched a king from another country and drew a conclusion about where God was, and moved house on the strength of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, with all their heart and with all their soul, but that whoever would not seek the LORD, the God of Israel, should be put to death, whether young or old, man or woman. They swore an oath to the LORD with a loud voice and with shouting and with trumpets and with horns. And all Judah rejoiced over the oath, for they had sworn with all their heart and had sought him with their whole desire, and he was found by them, and the LORD gave them rest all around.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What they do at the assembly is enter a covenant, and its content is a single verb.

And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, with all their heart and with all their soul.

Not to keep particular laws or fund particular works. To seek him — the word Asa had commanded at the start of the reign and Azariah had just preached — and to do it with the whole of themselves, in the language of the Shema.

And then verse 13, which is hard and should not be softened. But that whoever would not seek the LORD, the God of Israel, should be put to death, whether young or old, man or woman.

The warrant is in the law. Deuteronomy set the death penalty for apostasy in Israel — for the prophet who called the nation after other gods, for the family member who whispered it, for the man or woman found serving other gods within the gates. Asa's covenant is applying the statute of a covenant nation to itself by oath, and it is not an innovation.

It also does not transfer. That penalty belonged to one nation, under one covenant, in one land held on those terms, and the New Testament closes the door on carrying it forward in the plainest words available: the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, and the kingdom in question is not of this world, or its servants would fight. A church that reaches for verse 13 has misunderstood which covenant it is standing in.

What the covenant produced is in the next two verses, and it is noisy. They swore an oath to the LORD with a loud voice and with shouting and with trumpets and with horns. And all Judah rejoiced over the oath.

They were glad about it. A nation cheering as it binds itself is not a common sight, and the reason is given: they had sworn with all their heart and had sought him with their whole desire, and he was found by them, and the LORD gave them rest all around.

He was found by them. That is verse 2 delivered inside the same chapter — seek him and he will be found — and the Chronicler will not leave a reader wondering whether the promise held. It held, in thirteen verses.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even Maacah, his mother, King Asa removed from being queen mother because she had made a detestable image for Asherah; he cut it down, crushed it, and burned it at the brook Kidron (v. 16). But the high places were not taken out of Israel. Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true all his days (v. 17). He brings his father's sacred gifts and his own into the house of God (v. 18), and there was no more war until the thirty-fifth year of the reign of Asa (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The word even at the front of verse 16 is the Chronicler's comment. Reform reached the palace nursery, and the woman deposed was the king's own grandmother, holding the highest position a woman in Judah could hold.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 17 records a failure and a verdict in the same breath — the high places stood, and his heart was wholly true all his days. Scripture is measuring the direction of a life, not auditing it.

verseByVerse.quote: Even Maacah, his mother, King Asa removed from being queen mother because she had made a detestable image for Asherah. Asa cut down her image, crushed it, and burned it at the brook Kidron. But the high places were not taken out of Israel. Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true all his days. And he brought into the house of God the sacred gifts of his father and his own sacred gifts, silver, and gold, and vessels. And there was no more war until the thirty-fifth year of the reign of Asa.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even Maacah, his mother, King Asa removed from being queen mother because she had made a detestable image for Asherah.

The word even is the Chronicler's own. She is called his mother by the title of her office; she is in fact his grandmother, the woman Rehoboam loved above all his wives, the daughter of Absalom's line, who had put her own son Abijah on the throne ahead of the firstborn. Queen mother in Judah was a real position with real power, and she had held it through two reigns.

Asa takes it off her, and then goes further: Asa cut down her image, crushed it, and burned it at the brook Kidron. Three verbs, and the last of them is done in the valley below the city where the rubbish went, in public.

Reform is easy at a distance and expensive at the dinner table. This is the woman who raised his father and probably him, and he took her office away and burned her idol where everyone could watch.

Then verse 17, which puts a failure and a verdict in the same breath. But the high places were not taken out of Israel. Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true all his days.

Chapter 14 said he took the high places out of the cities of Judah; this says they were not taken out of Israel, which most likely refers to the northern territory he had annexed or to informal shrines that survived the purge. He did not finish. And the sentence that follows does not pretend he did — it grants the failure and then gives a verdict about the man rather than the audit: his heart was wholly true.

Hold that verdict, because the Chronicler has not yet written chapter 16, where this same king will buy a foreign army with temple silver, jail a prophet in the stocks, oppress his own people, and die of a disease in which he did not seek the LORD. All his days is still what stands here. Scripture is measuring the direction of a life and not tallying it, and it says both things about the same man without withdrawing either.

15.theology:
Verse 2 is 1 Chronicles 28:9 in a prophet's mouth. What David said privately to Solomon on the day he handed over the temple plans has become the standing terms of the dynasty, and the Spirit of God is what brought it back. Verse 15 then reports the promise kept inside the same chapter: they sought him with their whole desire, and he was found by them.

Azariah's history lesson names God as the author of the distress that produced the turning — God troubled them with every sort of distress — exactly the first-person claim of 7:13. The trouble was not an obstacle to the finding. It was the road to it.

The death penalty of verse 13 has its warrant in Deuteronomy's law for apostasy in a covenant nation, and it does not transfer. The weapons of the church's warfare are not of the flesh, and its King said plainly that if his kingdom were of this world his servants would fight.
15.examples:
The altar needed repair. Sixty years after fire came down on it in front of the whole nation, the stonework had been let go, in a working temple, with priests walking past it daily. Decline shows in the fabric first, and noticing it is already the beginning of the reform.

He deposed his own grandmother and burned her idol in the valley where the rubbish went. Reform is cheap at a distance and expensive at the dinner table.

Verse 17 grants that he never finished — the high places stood — and calls his heart wholly true all his days in the same breath. Scripture measures the direction of a life rather than auditing it.

16.title: The Eyes of the LORD Run to and Fro
