Sinclair Ferguson observes: "Manasseh's late repentance is genuine and was received by God — but the Chronicler is honest that genuine repentance does not restore everything that sin destroyed. Some seeds, once planted, grow beyond the one who planted them."

Amon his son (vv. 21–25) makes the worst possible choice in the worst possible way: he multiplied guilt like his father Manasseh but did not humble himself before the LORD as his father had humbled himself (v. 23). He had his father's sin but not his father's repentance. He was assassinated by his servants after only two years. The people of the land killed the conspirators and made Josiah king in his place — the generation is setting the stage for the last great reform king of the monarchy.

33.theology: The Limitless Reach of Repentance and Grace. Manasseh is the Chronicler's ultimate test case of 7:14: does God's offer of forgiveness for the one who humbles himself, prays, seeks, and turns have any limits? The answer chapter 33 gives is no. The worst king in Judah's history, arriving at genuine humility and prayer in a Babylonian dungeon, was heard by the God of heaven and restored. This is not a guarantee that all consequences are removed (they were not — the seeds of exile were already planted, and Josiah's reforms could only delay what Manasseh had set in motion). But it is the guarantee that no sin places a person beyond the reach of the God who is moved by genuine entreaty.
33.examples:
Then: The prophets who warned Manasseh for decades without being heard were not wasting their breath — the word they planted may have been part of what Manasseh remembered in Babylon when he turned to pray. The preached word does not always bear fruit in the first hearing; it does not return empty.

Now: The family member or friend who has prayed for a deeply wayward person for years without result has Manasseh's story to cling to. The God who heard the prayer of a man who had committed child sacrifice and filled the temple with idols can hear the prayer of any prodigal. The dungeon where the prayer is finally prayed may be as unlikely as Manasseh's Babylonian chains — but the God who received it is the same God.

34.title: His Heart Was Tender
34.text: "Because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before God when you heard his words against this place and its inhabitants, and you have humbled yourself before me and have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you, declares the LORD." (34:27)
34.overview: Josiah is the last great reform king and one of the most moving figures in 2 Chronicles. He begins seeking God at sixteen, begins destroying idols at twenty, and at twenty-six supervises the great temple repair that leads to the discovery of the Book of the Law. When the law is read to him, he tears his clothes and weeps — the response of a tender heart that recognizes the gap between what God requires and what has actually been done. The prophetess Huldah confirms that judgment is inevitable for Judah (the seeds planted by Manasseh have sprouted beyond recall) but that Josiah himself will be spared because of his tenderness. The chapter ends with Josiah gathering all Israel for the greatest covenant renewal since Moses.

sections.title: A Young King Seeks God (vv. 1–7)
sections.commentary:
Josiah begins at eight years old (v. 1), seeks the God of David at sixteen (v. 3), and at twenty begins the destruction of the Baal altars, Asherim, carved images, and metal images throughout Judah and Jerusalem, then extends the destruction into the north (v. 6–7 — Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, as far as Naphtali). The geographic scope of the reform — deliberately covering the same territory as the original united kingdom — signals that Josiah intends to restore the Davidic-Solomonic ideal, not merely to manage Judah's spiritual maintenance.

The burning of the bones of idolatrous priests on their own altars (v. 5) fulfills the specific prophecy of the unnamed man of God in 1 Kings 13:2 ("a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice on you the bones of men"). The prophecy was given at the very beginning of the northern kingdom's apostate worship — three hundred years earlier. Its fulfillment in Josiah is the Chronicler's demonstration that no word of God falls to the ground: even a prophecy three centuries old, naming the specific agent of its fulfillment, comes to pass exactly as spoken. Alistair Begg has observed: "Josiah did not know he was fulfilling a prophecy given three hundred years before his birth. He was simply obeying what was right. And God was fulfilling through his obedience what he had promised through the prophet."

sections.title: The Book of the Law Discovered (vv. 8–21)
sections.commentary:
The discovery of the Book of the Law during the temple repair is the pivotal moment of Josiah's reign and one of the most dramatic moments in Israel's history. Hilkiah the high priest finds the book (likely Deuteronomy, or a substantial portion of the Pentateuch) and gives it to Shaphan the secretary, who reads it and reports to the king, and then reads it in the king's hearing.

Josiah's response to the reading of the law is the response of a tender heart that actually hears God's word. He tears his clothes — the physical expression of grief and alarm (v. 19). He sends immediately to inquire of the LORD: "Go, inquire of the LORD for me and for those who are left in Israel and in Judah, concerning the words of the book that has been found. For great is the wrath of the LORD that is poured out on us, because our fathers have not kept the word of the LORD, to do according to all that is written in this book" (v. 21).

The tearing of clothes is the embodiment of the first condition of 7:14: humble yourself. Josiah has the authority to dismiss the newly discovered book as the work of some old priest, to manage its implications with political wisdom, to treat it as one input among many. Instead, he tears his clothes. He hears the word of God and is undone by it — by the distance between what God requires and what Judah has done.

R. C. Sproul often preached this passage as a model of genuine encounter with God's word: the man who hears the Bible preached and is comfortable has either perfectly met the law's requirements (impossible) or has not actually heard it. The word of God in its full weight, when genuinely heard, should produce in every honest heart something like what it produced in Josiah — the recognition of the gap between divine requirement and human performance, which is simultaneously the beginning of genuine repentance and the opening for genuine grace.

sections.title: Huldah's Oracle and the Covenant Renewal (vv. 22–33)
sections.commentary:
The delegation goes to Huldah the prophetess (v. 22) — a remarkable choice and a remarkable figure. Huldah is one of the five writing-free female prophets in the Old Testament (Miriam, Deborah, Huldah, Noadiah, and Philip's daughters), and she is apparently the prophet of highest authority in Jerusalem at this moment. The delegation from the king of Judah goes to a woman for the word of the LORD — and the Chronicler records her word without comment on the delegation's gender dynamics. The word that matters is not who speaks it but what it says.

Huldah's oracle has two parts: the judgment that is certain and the grace that is personal. The judgment (vv. 24–25) is irreversible: because Judah has forsaken God and burned incense to other gods, all the curses of the book will come upon this place. Manasseh's seeds have grown beyond harvest prevention. The exile is coming; no amount of reform will stop it now. But the personal grace (vv. 26–28) is equally certain: because Josiah's heart was tender (the Hebrew rak means soft, receptive, easily moved by God's word) and he humbled himself and wept before God, he will be gathered to his fathers in peace before the judgment falls. He will not see the disaster with his own eyes.

The covenant renewal (vv. 29–33) is the whole community gathered at the temple, the book read in their hearing, and Josiah standing at his pillar and making a covenant to walk after the LORD, to keep his commandments and testimonies with all his heart and all his soul. And all who were present in Jerusalem did accordingly (v. 32). For the rest of his lifetime, the people did not turn away from following the LORD the God of their fathers (v. 33). The reform is real, comprehensive, and sustained — because it is driven by a king whose heart is tender to the word of God.

Sinclair Ferguson notes that Huldah's word contains the deepest comfort and the deepest sorrow of the book simultaneously: the judgment that is certain and the mercy that is personal are both spoken in the same breath by the same prophet. This is the pattern of the gospel: the word that declares humanity under condemnation is the same word that announces the rescue of those who humble themselves and receive it.

34.theology: The Tender Heart and the Hard Word. Josiah's response to the Book of the Law — tearing his clothes, weeping, humbling himself — is the fulfillment of 7:14's second and third conditions in their most personal and immediate form. He hears the word of God and humbles himself before it, not as a calculated political move but as the instinctive response of a heart that has been seeking God since the age of sixteen. The tenderness that receives the word is the fruit of years of seeking — it does not arise spontaneously in the moment of crisis but is the characteristic response of a heart formed by sustained devotion to God.
34.examples:
Then: Josiah at the reading of the law is the model of every person who hears the word of God and is genuinely moved by it — not merely informed, not merely impressed, but broken and undone by the recognition of the distance between what God requires and what they have been. This breaking is not the end; it is the beginning of the grace that flows to the humble.

Now: The recovery of serious, systematic, expository preaching in the church — the kind that reads the whole counsel of God rather than selecting the comfortable portions — is the institutional form of what happened to Josiah. When God's people hear the full weight of what God requires and what the gospel provides, tearing of clothes (metaphorical or otherwise) is the appropriate response.

35.title: No Passover Like It
35.text: "No Passover like it had been kept in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet. None of the kings of Israel had kept such a Passover as was kept by Josiah." (35:18)
35.overview: Chapter 35 records Josiah's great Passover — surpassing even Hezekiah's in the specific comparison to Samuel rather than Solomon — and then, shockingly, his premature and tragic death at Megiddo. Pharaoh Neco is marching north to fight at Carchemish; he sends word to Josiah to stand aside because "God has commanded me to hurry"; Josiah does not listen and disguises himself to fight. He is fatally wounded by archers. The grief of all Israel, including Jeremiah's lament, is the most extensive mourning scene in the book. The best king in Judah's history dies at thirty-nine, his work unfinished, killed in a battle he should not have fought. The mystery of the godly man's untimely death is left as mystery — the Chronicler offers no theodicy, only grief.

sections.title: The Great Passover: Beyond Hezekiah and Samuel (vv. 1–19)
sections.commentary:
Josiah's Passover (14th of Nisan, the proper month — unlike Hezekiah's second-month celebration) is organized with meticulous liturgical care. He appoints the priests to their offices (v. 2), encourages them (v. 2), commands the Levites who taught all Israel (v. 3 — the teaching function of the Levites, established by Jehoshaphat in ch. 17, is still operative), and instructs them to carry the ark no longer on their shoulders (v. 3 — the ark is permanently at rest in the temple; the Levites' carrying function is now the teaching and service of the people).

The provision is astonishing: thirty thousand lambs and young goats, three thousand bulls — all from the king's own resources (vv. 7–9). The Passover lambs are slaughtered according to strict order: the Levites kill the Passover lamb for everyone (v. 11), maintaining ritual propriety at scale. The fire-offerings are boiled and apportioned rapidly (v. 13) — the entire priestly and Levitical organization running at peak efficiency in service of the massive celebration.

The comparison to Samuel (v. 18) rather than Solomon (Hezekiah's comparison, 30:26) is significant: Josiah's Passover surpasses even the comparison that flattered Hezekiah's, reaching back further in history to the era of Samuel — the last great pre-monarchic judge-prophet who had organized Israel's worship. Dale Ralph Davis notes that Samuel was the bridge between the judges and the kings, the man who anointed the first Davidic king and who maintained the proper worship of the LORD when the Elide priesthood had corrupted it. To surpass Samuel's Passover is to reach back before the monarchy's failures to the era of the judges' best moments — a claim of unparalleled covenant faithfulness.

Alistair Begg observes that Josiah's Passover is the Old Testament's last great celebration of the foundational act of redemption before the exile scatters God's people. The lamb is slaughtered one final time in the great gathering of all Israel in the land — and then the shadow falls. The next generation will keep the Passover in Babylon, by memory and grief. The Passover that follows this one is the one Jesus will eat with his disciples on the night he was betrayed — at which he will take the bread and the cup and say, "This is my body... this is my blood... do this in remembrance of me." Josiah's Passover is the last great rehearsal; Jesus' Passover is the fulfillment.

sections.title: The Tragic Death at Megiddo (vv. 20–25)
sections.commentary:
Pharaoh Neco's message to Josiah is one of the most theologically complex moments in the chapter: "What have we to do with each other, king of Judah? I am not coming against you this day, but against the house with which I am at war. And God has commanded me to hurry. Stop opposing God, who is with me, lest he destroy you" (v. 21). A pagan pharaoh claiming to speak for God. Josiah ignores the warning and disguises himself to fight.

The mystery is acute: was Neco telling the truth? The text says "Josiah would not turn away from him, but disguised himself in order to fight with him. He did not listen to the words of Neco from the mouth of God" (v. 22). The phrase "from the mouth of God" strongly implies that the warning was genuinely from God, that Josiah's failure to listen was a failure to hear God's word through an unlikely instrument. R. C. Sproul wrestled with this: "God can speak through Balaam's donkey, through Cyrus the Persian king, through Pilate. The question is not whether the instrument is worthy but whether the message is true. Josiah's failure to listen to Neco's warning is the single moment in an otherwise magnificent reign where the tender heart fails to hear."

Josiah is mortally wounded by archers, carried to Jerusalem, and dies there. The grief is comprehensive and unprecedented: all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah; Jeremiah uttered a lament for him; all the singing men and women have spoken of Josiah in their laments to this day; it became a rule in Israel (v. 24–25). The lament for Josiah — Israel's best king, dead at thirty-nine in a battle he shouldn't have fought — is one of the Bible's most poignant grief-scenes. Michael Wilcock observes: "The Chronicler offers no explanation for why the righteous die prematurely. He simply records the grief. Some things cannot be explained; they can only be mourned."

sections.title: The End of a Reign: The Best and the Incomplete (v. 26–27)
sections.commentary:
The brief summary (vv. 26–27) — his acts of devotion according to what is written in the Law of the LORD, his deeds first and last — closes a reign that was both the height of Israel's covenant fidelity and the occasion of profound grief. Josiah did what no king before him had done in the specificity and thoroughness of his seeking and reforming; and he died too young, in a battle that God apparently did not authorize.

The mystery of Josiah's death is not resolved by the Chronicler, and any commentary that tries to resolve it is wiser than the text. What the text does is place his death between the greatest Passover in Israel's history (v. 18) and the beginning of the final collapse of the monarchy (ch. 36). The good shepherd who celebrated the foundational redemption more completely than anyone since Samuel is gone, and what remains is a Judah without its best king, facing the most powerful empires in the world without the one who knew how to pray and seek and humble himself before God.

The death of Josiah at Megiddo haunts Israel's memory — and will haunt the eschatological imagination of Zechariah (Zech. 12:11, "the mourning of Megiddo") as a type of grief for the pierced one whose loss will be the occasion for the greatest national mourning in history. The grief at Megiddo points forward to the grief of Good Friday — and Good Friday points forward to the resurrection that turns all grief to joy.

35.theology: The Untimely Death of the Righteous. Josiah's death is 2 Chronicles' most theologically challenging moment: the best king, the most faithful reformer, the man who wept at the word of God — cut down at thirty-nine in a battle God apparently warned him not to fight. The Chronicler offers no resolution. The book does not say "God permitted this to accomplish a greater purpose." It simply records the death and the grief. The Christian reading this through the lens of the resurrection understands something Josiah's mourners did not: the death of the righteous is not the final word. Josiah was "gathered to his fathers in peace" (Huldah's word, 34:28) — and the God who gathered him knows what he does with the tender hearts of those who served him well.
35.examples:
Then: Jeremiah's lament for Josiah (mentioned in v. 25) is the prophet's own grief over a king who had been his ally and the community's best hope. The prophet who would soon preach judgment on Jerusalem was weeping for the king who had delayed that judgment. This is the complexity of prophetic ministry: speaking both the hard word of judgment and the genuine word of grief.

Now: The early deaths of faithful ministers, missionaries, and Christians — those who seem to have been most needed and most fruitful — raise the same question Josiah raises. The Chronicler's answer is not an explanation but a posture: grieve, honor the memory, keep the lament alive, and trust the God who gathers the righteous to himself.

36.title: Let Him Go Up
36.text: "Thus says Cyrus king of Persia, 'The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whoever is among you of all his people, may the LORD his God be with him. Let him go up.'" (36:23)
36.overview: The final chapter of 2 Chronicles — and of the Hebrew Bible in its Jewish canonical ordering — compresses the last four kings of Judah (Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, Zedekiah) into a rapid, grief-filled descent to exile. The Babylonian exile is not the Chronicler's final word; his final word is Cyrus's decree. After the destruction of the temple and the deportation of the people, after the land keeps its sabbaths in silence, the LORD stirs the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia. And Cyrus's last word — the last word of the book, the last word of the Hebrew Bible — is ya'al: let him go up. The exile is not the end. Ascent is the final word. The gate is open. Let him go up.

sections.title: The Last Four Kings: A Nation in Free Fall (vv. 1–14)
sections.commentary:
The four final kings of Judah are treated in rapid succession, the Chronicler's narrative accelerating like a stone rolling downhill. Jehoahaz reigns three months and is taken to Egypt by Pharaoh Neco (vv. 2–4). Jehoiakim reigns eleven years, bound in bronze chains by Nebuchadnezzar, temple vessels taken to Babylon (vv. 5–8). Jehoiachin reigns three months and ten days, taken to Babylon with more temple vessels (vv. 9–10). Zedekiah reigns eleven years, hardens his heart, stiffens his neck, refuses to turn to the LORD (vv. 11–13).

The verdict on each is the same variation: "he did evil in the sight of the LORD his God." The trajectory established in chapter 10 by Rehoboam's folly has been descending for sixteen chapters, interrupted by the great reform kings (Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joash, Hezekiah, Josiah) but never fully arrested. Now the descent is complete and vertical. The last kings make Rehoboam look restrained.

The summary of the leadership failure (v. 14) is comprehensive: the chief priests and the people likewise were exceedingly unfaithful (ma'al), following all the abominations of the nations, polluting the house of the LORD. This is the ma'al principle reaching its terminus: the cumulative unfaithful breach of covenant has produced the cumulative covenant curse. Deuteronomy 28 is being fulfilled. Dale Ralph Davis observes that the compression of four reigns into fourteen verses is itself the Chronicler's comment: these kings are not worth detailed treatment because they have nothing to teach except the terrible lesson that some trajectories cannot be reversed by anything short of catastrophe.

sections.title: The Mercies Rejected, the Judgment Executed (vv. 15–21)
sections.commentary:
The Chronicler's most explicit theological assessment of the exile (vv. 15–16) is both the saddest and most merciful statement in the book: "The LORD, the God of their fathers, sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place. But they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words and scoffing at his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD rose against his people, until there was no remedy."

"He had compassion" — the Hebrew hemla describes the tender, parental compassion of God for his people. He did not want to send the judgment; he sent messengers precisely because he did not want to execute it. He kept sending them — the persistence of the mercy is one of the most moving details in the chapter. Prophet after prophet, generation after generation, until the account of mercy was so thoroughly refused that no more remedy was possible. Alistair Begg has preached this as the New Testament gospel from the Old Testament perspective: God's persistence in offering mercy before judgment is the character of the God who "so loved the world that he gave his only Son" and who is "not willing that any should perish but that all should come to repentance" (2 Pet. 3:9). The exile is the consequence of mercy persistently refused.

The destruction of the temple and Jerusalem (vv. 17–19) is described in spare, stark terms: the Chaldeans burn the house of God, break down the wall of Jerusalem, burn all its palaces with fire, and destroy all its precious vessels. The glory-cloud that filled the house in chapter 5, the fire that fell on the sacrifices in chapter 7, the gold that covered every wall — all gone. The house is a ruin; the city is a heap. The lamp of David has apparently gone out.

The land keeping its Sabbaths (v. 21) is one of the Chronicler's most theologically freighted details. Leviticus 26:34–35 had warned that if Israel was unfaithful, the land would keep its Sabbaths in exile — getting the rest it had been denied by Israel's refusal to observe the sabbath years. Now the land gets what God required: seventy years of silence, rest, and emptiness. The judgment is not random; it is the precise execution of the covenant's stated terms. Sinclair Ferguson notes: "Even in the exile, the law is being kept — just not by the people. The land is keeping its Sabbaths. God's word is being fulfilled even in judgment."

sections.title: Cyrus's Decree: Let Him Go Up (vv. 22–23)
sections.commentary:
"Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia" (v. 22). Two prophets are invoked in this verse: Jeremiah (whose prophecy of seventy years of exile, Jer. 25:11–12, 29:10, is being fulfilled) and implicitly Isaiah (who prophesied Cyrus by name two centuries before his birth, Isa. 44:28, 45:1). The exile's end was not a political accident or Persia's cultural generosity; it was the fulfillment of the word of the LORD spoken through his prophets decades and centuries before it happened.

The LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus — the same verb used of the Spirit's movement throughout Chronicles. The Spirit who came on Azariah (15:1), on Jahaziel (20:14), on Zechariah (24:20) now moves in the heart of a Persian king. God's sovereignty is not limited to the covenant community; he stirs the spirit of whoever he chooses to accomplish his purposes. R. C. Sproul observes: "Cyrus never sought the God of Israel. He was moved by the God of Israel to serve the God of Israel's purposes — and he did so, making perhaps the most important proclamation a Gentile king ever made: let him go up."

Cyrus's proclamation attributes his authority to "the LORD, the God of heaven" — remarkable language for a Persian king, who would have understood himself as the servant of Ahura Mazda. Whether Cyrus had genuine theological clarity or was using politic language that resonated with his Jewish subjects, the Chronicler's point is unmistakable: the God who controlled Rehoboam's folly, who sent the Assyrians against Israel, who stirred up Nebuchadnezzar against Jerusalem, now stirs the spirit of the king of Persia to send his people home.

The final word of Cyrus — and the final word of the book — is "let him go up" (ya'al). In the Hebrew idiom, going up to Jerusalem is the natural language of pilgrimage and return (cf. Ps. 122:4, "the tribes go up... to give thanks to the name of the LORD"). But in this context, it is also the word of release from captivity, the word of resurrection from the death of exile, the word that opens the gate and says: the darkness is over, the captivity is ended, go up. Alistair Begg observes: "The last word of 2 Chronicles — and of the Hebrew Bible — is not the exile, not the ruins, not the weeping by the rivers of Babylon. It is ya'al: let him go up. The Bible that began with God creating a world ends with God opening a gate. The story is not over. The upward call is the last word."

For the Christian reading with resurrection eyes, ya'al is more than a permit to return to Jerusalem. It is the charter of every upward movement in salvation history: the resurrection of Jesus that declares the captivity of death over, the ascension that leads the train of captives on high (Eph. 4:8), the final summons to the City whose builder and maker is God. The exile of sin is over for all who are in Christ. The gate is open. Let him go up.

36.theology: The Upward Summons: The Bible's Last Word. 2 Chronicles ends — and the Hebrew Bible ends — with an open gate and an upward call. After the darkness of the exile, after the ruins of the temple, after the seventy years of Sabbath silence, the word that breaks the silence is not a philosophical explanation of why it all happened but a practical, urgent, hope-filled summons: let him go up. This is the gospel's structure in miniature: judgment is real, exile is real, darkness is real — and then the word comes that overturns it all, not by denying the darkness but by announcing that the light has broken through. Cyrus's decree is the Old Testament's closest analogue to the resurrection announcement: the captivity is over, the way home is open, rise and go.
36.examples:
Then: The exiles by the rivers of Babylon who had wept when they remembered Zion (Ps. 137) heard Cyrus's decree as the return of everything they thought lost. The seventy years of Sabbath silence became the soil out of which a chastened, purified, scripture-focused community of faith emerged — the community that would produce the synagogue, the rabbinic tradition, the faithful remnant that waited for the consolation of Israel. Exile did not destroy God's people; it refined them.

Now: Every person in Christ is living in the good of Cyrus's decree — the captivity to sin and death has been ended by the one greater than Cyrus, the true Son of David who died for sin and rose on the third day. The gate is open. The upward call has been issued. "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matt. 11:28). "Let him go up" — the last word of the Hebrew Bible — is the first word of the gospel: the exile is over, the way home is open, come.
